evidence: The worked example immediately above states 'TTFT budget 1.2 s, TPOT ~25 ms/token'; the bullet then uses '2 s SLO breach'. A reader cannot tell whether the SLO is 1.2 s, 2 s, or two different thresholds.
root_cause: Stale or undefined SLO value; likely a leftover from an earlier canonical workload.
correction: Use the canonical 1.2 s TTFT SLO consistently. If 2 s is a separate breach threshold or a different workload, define it explicitly and label it.
acceptance_test: Search every TTFT/SLO mention in Ch 11 and the canonical-workload table; exactly one canonical TTFT SLO value is used, and any second threshold is explicitly defined.

quoted_clause: allocates KV in fixed blocks shared and evicted like page frames
observed: The wording implies general cross-request block sharing, which is not PagedAttention's core mechanism; sharing is an optional copy-on-write/prefix-reuse feature.
evidence: The chapter's mental model correctly says PagedAttention reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation, while prefix caching separately dedupes shared prefixes. Table 11-1 also separates PagedAttention from prefix caching.
root_cause: Imprecise wording blurs PagedAttention's block-mapping mechanism with prefix/KV sharing.
correction: Say that PagedAttention allocates KV in fixed-size blocks mapped through a per-request block table; blocks may be shared only when the engine implements copy-on-write or prefix reuse.
acceptance_test: The paragraph does not attribute prefix-sharing benefits to PagedAttention alone; PagedAttention and prefix caching remain distinguishable from the text.

page_hint: Ch 11 §1, paragraph after the four mechanisms
quoted_clause: P/D disaggregation makes it scale.
observed: This is an unqualified universal claim. The same chapter later says P/D disaggregation is premature for the canonical single-host and pays off only when measured prefill/decode interference binds.
evidence: Ch 11 §3 states: 'For the canonical single-host (~10 rps) this disaggregation is premature; it pays off when measured prefill/decode interference binds'. Table 11-1 also scopes it to 'workload outgrows a node'.
root_cause: Summary sentence overstates a conditional optimization.
correction: Replace with: 'P/D disaggregation can improve goodput at scale when measured phase interference and KV-transfer/orchestration costs justify it.'
acceptance_test: No unqualified 'makes it scale' remains; the sentence states the condition and the transfer/orchestration cost.

page_hint: Ch 11 §1 item 4 and Ch 11 §3 'When to Disaggregate'
quoted_clause: reports up to 525% throughput lift ... reported up to 525% long-context throughput
observed: One formulation says 'throughput lift'; the other says 'throughput'. A 525% figure can mean 5.25× baseline or 6.25× baseline, and the two sentences do not resolve which.
evidence: The same source is described twice with different grammar; the later sentence adds 'a lift over the paper's own baseline configuration' but still does not state the multiplier unambiguously.
root_cause: Ambiguous percentage wording carried across two locations.
correction: State the baseline and multiplier explicitly, e.g. 'up to 525% higher throughput (6.25× baseline)' or '5.25× baseline', whichever matches the paper, and use the same formulation in both places.
acceptance_test: Both locations use the same unambiguous formulation; no bare '525% throughput' remains without 'higher/lift' and a stated baseline.

quoted_clause: Measure KV utilization — fraction of the 640 GB node memory consumed by live KV vs weights.
observed: KV utilization is not the fraction of total node memory consumed by live KV versus weights. It is used KV capacity divided by available KV capacity (or live KV bytes divided by the KV budget).
evidence: The same item then says 'PagedAttention raises effective KV packing (block utilization); prefix caching instead dedupes shared prefixes (prefix-hit rate) — track the two separately', which presumes a KV-capacity denominator, not total node memory.
root_cause: Conflates a whole-node memory breakdown with the KV-cache utilization metric.
correction: Define KV utilization as allocated/live KV blocks divided by total KV block capacity, or live KV bytes divided by the KV budget. Report weights, activations, workspace, and other memory separately.
acceptance_test: The metric definition has the correct denominator and excludes weights; no 'vs weights' phrasing remains in the KV-utilization definition.

quoted_clause: Requests that exit at different iterations can leave an initially uniform batch with different amounts of remaining computation.
observed: Early exit is per-token, not per-request. A request contains many tokens, each of which may exit at a different depth; the scheduler's unit of work is the token/sequence state, not a request-level exit.
evidence: The preceding sentence explicitly defines 'Adaptive depth (per-token early exit — the same early-exit interface above)'.
root_cause: Unit-of-work confusion between requests and tokens.
correction: Say: 'Tokens that exit at different iterations can leave a batch with different remaining computation per sequence; a request may contain a mix of depths.'
acceptance_test: The paragraph consistently uses token-level exit; no request-level early-exit claim remains unless the model explicitly supports request-level exit.

page_hint: Ch 10 §7, second bullet on 2026 MoE scaling
quoted_clause: the all-to-all routing it forces
observed: Expert parallelism can require all-to-all communication when experts are distributed across devices, but not all MoE serving uses EP or all-to-all. Replicated experts, expert caching, or other placements can avoid it.
evidence: The same bullet says EP and fused cross-expert communication kernels are 'increasingly central', which is a deployment choice, not a forced property of every MoE.
root_cause: Causal overstatement: a common EP consequence is presented as a universal MoE requirement.
correction: Say 'the all-to-all routing it can require when experts are distributed across devices' and acknowledge alternative placements.
acceptance_test: No 'forces' claim remains without a condition; the text acknowledges at least one alternative to all-to-all EP.

page_hint: Ch 10 §7, second bullet on 2026 MoE scaling
quoted_clause: the total expert residency that must be sharded ... since the full expert set occupies HBM even when only a fraction is routed per token
observed: The text assumes all experts must be resident in HBM. Large-MoE serving can offload or cache experts, so total residency is a deployment assumption, not a universal law.
evidence: The same bullet correctly distinguishes active parameters from total parameters; that distinction is exactly why residency policy matters. EP sharding is one policy, not the only one.
root_cause: Unstated assumption that all experts are HBM-resident.
correction: Add the condition: 'if the deployment requires all experts resident; otherwise expert offloading/caching changes the capacity calculus.'
acceptance_test: The text states the all-experts-resident assumption and does not present it as a universal MoE property.

quoted_clause: Within each node, the MoE active weights are small ... checked against the node's 640 GB HBM
observed: Active weights determine compute per token, not memory residency. The mini-case appears to use active weights as a residency check, then separately says EP shards total residency.
evidence: The next clause says 'EP to shard the total expert set (EP shards total residency, not the active count)'. That is the correct memory constraint, but the preceding sentence uses active weights against node HBM.
root_cause: Conflates active-parameter compute footprint with total-parameter memory residency.
correction: Compute total resident bytes per node after EP sharding and compare that to 640 GB. Use active parameters only for compute/FLOPs, not for the HBM residency check.
acceptance_test: The mini-case shows total resident bytes per node ≤ 640 GB; active-parameter bytes are not used as the residency check.

quoted_clause: the mechanism makes the GPU the steady bottleneck instead of the scheduler.
observed: Continuous batching does not guarantee that the GPU becomes the steady bottleneck. Insufficient arrivals, KV capacity, prefill/decode interference, and scheduling policy can still bind.
evidence: The same paragraph already says 'idle can still occur from insufficient arrivals, KV capacity, prefill, or scheduling policy'.
root_cause: Overstrong causal claim contradicted by the paragraph's own caveats.
correction: Say that continuous batching can shift the bottleneck from batch-boundary idle time toward GPU resources when arrivals and KV capacity permit, while scheduler policy can still bind.
acceptance_test: No universal 'makes the GPU the steady bottleneck' claim remains; the conditions and remaining scheduler constraints are stated.

quoted_clause: retrieved 2026-10-28 UTC; implementation observation outside the 2026-08-30 snapshot ... outside the book's 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff
observed: Several footnotes rely on sources retrieved 2026-10-27/28, after the stated 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff.
evidence: The footnote text itself gives the retrieval dates and explicitly labels at least one source as outside the cutoff.
root_cause: Evidence-cutoff policy is either not consistently applied or not explicitly exceptioned.
correction: Either update the cutoff, or state an exception policy explaining why these implementation observations do not affect time-sensitive claims; pin revisions within the cutoff where possible.
acceptance_test: Every source date is ≤ the cutoff or is explicitly listed as a post-cutoff exception with rationale; no claim depends on post-cutoff evidence without a label.

quoted_clause: C ≈ 17.5 (the 436 GB canonical KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token whole-context request)
observed: The quotient is arithmetically consistent only if 24.9 GB is the FP16 KV footprint for 9,500 tokens (9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB). At the book's 8-bit canonical KV rate (1.31 MB/token), 9,500 tokens is ≈12.4 GB, giving C ≈ 35, not 17.5. The chunk never states which KV precision the 436 GB budget and the 24.9 GB per-request figure use.
evidence: House convention: 8-bit KV ≈ 1.31 MB/token; FP16 KV ≈ 2.62 MB/token at the canonical 70B full-MHA reference. 9,500 × 2.62 MB = 24.89 GB; 436/24.89 = 17.52. 9,500 × 1.31 MB = 12.445 GB; 436/12.445 = 35.03. The text's '24.9 GB' therefore silently selects FP16 while the surrounding canonical discussion does not label the precision.
root_cause: Precision assumption is omitted from a canonical KV quotient, so the reader cannot tell whether 436 GB and 24.9 GB are both FP16, both 8-bit, or mixed. If the canonical budget is 8-bit, the stated C is off by ~2× and every downstream slot/throughput number in this example is wrong.
correction: State the KV precision explicitly in the quotient, e.g. 'C ≈ 17.5 FP16-KV request-equivalents (436 GB FP16 KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token request)' or, if the canonical budget is 8-bit, recompute to C ≈ 35 and update the 17-slot, 1.98 req/s, 2.03 req/s, and ~3% gap figures consistently. Add a one-line sanity check: 9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB (FP16) or 9,500 × 1.31 MB ≈ 12.4 GB (8-bit).
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 436/24.9 = 17.5 from the stated precision and token count without guessing; if 8-bit is intended, the same reader reproduces 436/12.4 ≈ 35 and the downstream slot/throughput numbers are updated everywhere.

page_hint: Ch 14, §3 Step 2 result worksheet, KV allocator usage row
quoted_clause: C ≈ 17.5 whole-context slots/host
observed: The prose immediately above says the quotient 'gives at most 17 whole-context slots, not a deployable concurrency of 17.5' and distinguishes 'floor 17 for provisioning, 17.5 for analysis.' The worksheet then labels C ≈ 17.5 as 'whole-context slots/host,' reintroducing the fractional-slot language the prose just rejected.
evidence: Same section: 'gives at most 17 whole-context slots, not a deployable concurrency of 17.5' and 'floor 17 for provisioning, 17.5 for analysis.' The table row uses 'slots' for the analytical quotient, which is not an integer slot count.

page_hint: Ch 14, §3 Step 2 result worksheet, Hardware utilization row
quoted_clause: achieved FLOP/s ÷ peak FLOP/s (MFU, Ch 8 definition)
observed: MFU is normally model FLOPs utilization: model FLOPs divided by (peak FLOP/s × elapsed time), not achieved FLOP/s divided by peak FLOP/s. The latter is an achieved-FLOP/s utilization or hardware utilization metric. The parenthetical '(MFU, Ch 8 definition)' may be relying on a local definition, but the formula as printed is not the standard MFU definition and can mislead readers who know the standard term.
evidence: Standard usage: MFU = model FLOPs / (peak FLOP/s × time). Achieved FLOP/s ÷ peak FLOP/s measures all achieved floating-point work, including non-model overhead, and is not the same quantity. The chunk does not restate Ch 8's definition, so the row is ambiguous at this location.
root_cause: The worksheet uses 'MFU' as a label for a ratio that is not MFU under the usual definition, without a local formula that resolves the ambiguity.
correction: Either write the Ch 8 formula explicitly in the row (e.g. 'model FLOPs ÷ (peak FLOP/s × elapsed time), per Ch 8') or rename the row to 'Achieved FLOP/s utilization' and keep MFU as a separate metric if both are recorded.
acceptance_test: A reader who knows the standard MFU definition can tell whether the row records MFU or achieved-FLOP/s utilization, and the Ch 8 cross-reference resolves to the same formula.

quoted_clause: Bigger batch sizes raise tokens/s but push TTFT over the deadline, zeroing goodput
observed: The bullet states a universal causal chain: bigger batch → TTFT over deadline → goodput zero. In practice, larger batches can raise throughput while only some requests miss the SLO; goodput falls but is not necessarily zero. It becomes zero only if no request meets the SLO over the measurement window.
evidence: Goodput is SLO-compliant throughput. If a batch increase pushes p95 TTFT over the deadline but some requests still meet it, goodput is positive but lower. The text's own definition of goodput (Ch 6) does not imply that any SLO breach zeroes it.
root_cause: Claim strength exceeds the mechanism: a conditional degradation is written as an unconditional zeroing.
correction: Replace with 'can push TTFT over the deadline and reduce goodput, potentially to zero if no request in the window meets the SLO' or similar conditional wording.
acceptance_test: The corrected bullet no longer asserts that any batch-induced TTFT breach zeroes goodput; it states the condition under which goodput reaches zero.

quoted_clause: measure chars/token with the model's own tokenizer; no Ch 6 figure is cited
observed: The parenthetical 'no Ch 6 figure is cited' is an internal review/editorial note, not reader-facing prose. It interrupts the measurement instruction and reads as a response to a prior review rather than part of the handbook.
evidence: The surrounding sentence is instructional: 'The "4 chars ≈ 1 token" estimate can be ~1.5–3× off for code/JSON/technical text (measure chars/token with the model's own tokenizer; no Ch 6 figure is cited).' The final clause has no pedagogical function for the reader.
root_cause: Review-response residue left in the manuscript.
correction: Remove 'no Ch 6 figure is cited' or replace it with a substantive cross-reference if a Ch 6 figure is actually relevant. Keep the instruction to measure with the model's own tokenizer.
acceptance_test: The sentence reads as handbook prose with no meta-review language; any cross-reference points to material the reader can use.

quoted_clause: Two models with identical MMLU can differ wildly in TTFT under the same batching, because serving depends on tokenizer, context length, KV layout, and scheduler — none of which a leaderboard scores.
observed: The causal list omits model size, architecture, and hardware, which are first-order determinants of TTFT. 'Identical MMLU' does not hold model size constant; two models with the same MMLU can have very different parameter counts and therefore very different TTFT even with the same tokenizer, context length, KV layout, and scheduler.
evidence: TTFT is dominated by prefill compute and memory traffic, which scale with model size and architecture. The sentence's 'because' list is presented as the explanation, but it is incomplete in a way that could let a reader infer that tokenizer/context/KV/scheduler are the only relevant variables.
root_cause: The illustrative list is written as an exhaustive causal explanation.
correction: Add 'model size and architecture, hardware, and batching policy' to the list, or soften to 'among other factors, serving depends on tokenizer, context length, KV layout, scheduler, model size, and hardware.'
acceptance_test: The sentence no longer implies that tokenizer, context length, KV layout, and scheduler are the only reasons identical-MMLU models can differ in TTFT.

quoted_clause: They do NOT tell us how fast, how cheap, or how it behaves under our traffic — model capability is the goal (Ch4's Quality dimension) — the quality gate — while deployment benchmarks measure the constraints (latency, throughput, cost) that capability benchmarks do not; if capability fails its quality gate (Ch 12's candidate (c)), it becomes the binding constraint before any serving optimization.
observed: The sentence is a long dash-chained construction with three nested asides. It is grammatically difficult and forces the reader to reconstruct the main contrast between capability and deployment benchmarks.
evidence: The core claim is simple: capability benchmarks answer quality; deployment benchmarks answer system behavior. The sentence embeds that contrast inside multiple em-dash qualifications and a semicolon clause.
root_cause: Overloaded sentence structure, not a technical error.
correction: Split into two or three sentences: one for what capability benchmarks answer, one for what they do not answer, one for the quality-gate consequence. Keep the Ch 4 and Ch 12 cross-references but attach them to the relevant clause.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the subject and predicate of the main contrast on first reading without backtracking through dashes.

quoted_clause: with §6 FP8-KV decision, ⌈344/35⌉ = 10 hosts at 40 rps, bounded below by the ~7-host prefill requirement — prefill compute then binds
observed: The ~7-host prefill requirement is inconsistent with Ch 17's independent prefill screen at 40 rps: 19 hosts under case (i), 21 under case (iii), 22 under case (ii), all at 35% MFU. The ~7-host figure corresponds to the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (368,000 ÷ 56,500 ≈ 6.5), not the stated 35% MFU screen. If the prefill requirement were ~7 and the FP8-KV screen were 10, prefill would not bind; KV would.
evidence: Ch 17 §4 and Table 17-2 state the 40-rps prefill screen as 19/21/22 hosts under cases (i)/(iii)/(ii). Ch 15 §6 itself defines 56,500 tok/s as the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling, not the 35%-MFU prefill screen.
root_cause: Mixing the 100%-MFU impossibility check with the 35%-MFU prefill screen and mislabeling which screen binds.
correction: Replace the ~7-host figure with the Ch 17 prefill screen under the stated FLOP-counting case (19 under case (i), 21 under case (iii), 22 under case (ii)) and state that the FP8-KV screen of 10 is below the prefill screen, so prefill binds.

quoted_clause: prefill demand ÷ host peak | 0.33× | 1.63× | 6.51×
observed: These ratios use 56,500 tok/s as the host prefill peak (100% MFU). Ch 17's canonical prefill screen uses 19,780 tok/s at 35% MFU, which gives 0.93×, 4.65×, and 18.6× for the same 2/10/40 rps cases. The table's denominator is unstated and inconsistent with the book's canonical prefill screen.
evidence: Ch 17 §4: 2.0 req/s × 9,200 = 18,400 input tokens/s; 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93%. Ch 15 §3 and §6 define 56,500 tok/s as the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling.

quoted_clause: canonical-price point at $20.80 per 1M tokens (≈$0.0208 per 1K-token request)

The arithmetic in the chapter uses $0.0208 per request, which is $20.80 per 1,000 requests.

observed: The caption conflates the N−1 reserve with case (ii). Under Table 17-1, 21 is the zero-spare KV screen; 22 is either the 95% scheduling-factor zero-spare screen or the case (ii) zero-spare compute screen; the N−1 reserve under the 70%×95% policy is 32 for KV-only and 34 for case (ii).

quoted_clause: 58 vs 31 — ~18–27 extra hosts
observed: The text says the mixed fleet needs '~18–27 extra hosts' relative to the single-model fleet, but the stated comparison is 58 vs 31, which is exactly 27 extra. The lower bound of 18 is unexplained.

quoted_clause: W_reuse(3) ≈ 14.14 s ... ~14.16 s with prefix reuse ... ~14.16 s
observed: The text derives W_reuse(3) ≈ 14.14 s from the stated 100%-prefix-reuse policy (incremental prefix 9,200 + 3×800 = 11,600), but the same section and Table 19-1 print ~14.16 s. The 14.16 value corresponds to using 11,795 (the full retained context) instead of 11,600.

quoted_clause: queue depth 200 × 1 = 200 requests, drained at ~50 rps in ~4 s
observed: The formula in the same sentence says 'buffer depth D·(200−r) requests' = 1 × (200−50) = 150 requests, and 'max queue wait ≈ D·(200−r)/r' = 1 × 150/50 = 3 s. The worked example instead uses 200 requests and ~4 s, which is the total arrivals and total drain time, not the excess buffer and max queue wait.
evidence: §23.8: 'max queue wait ≈ D·(200−r)/r must stay inside the 3 s SLO — so state D, the buffer depth D·(200−r) requests ... worked: D = 1 s at 200 rps → queue depth 200 × 1 = 200 requests, drained at ~50 rps in ~4 s'.
root_cause: Confusion between total arrivals (200) and excess buffer (150), and between total drain time (4 s) and max queue wait (3 s).
correction: Change 'queue depth 200 × 1 = 200 requests, drained at ~50 rps in ~4 s' to 'buffer depth 1 × (200−50) = 150 requests, drained at ~50 rps in ~3 s'.

quoted_clause: 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 in-flight × 24.9 GB ÷ 436 GB = 19.7 → 21 hosts (Ch 17)
observed: The arithmetic yields 19.65 (printed as 19.7), but the result is stated as 21 hosts. A clean ceil of 19.7 is 20, not 21. The FP8 analogue later in the same chapter explicitly writes '+N−1' (9.8 + 1 → 11), but this FP16 line omits the +N−1 step, so the reader cannot see how 19.7 becomes 21.
evidence: 344 × 24.9 = 8565.6; 8565.6 ÷ 436 = 19.65. ceil(19.65) = 20. To reach 21 requires an additional +1 (N−1) step: 19.65 + 1 = 20.65 → 21. The text does not state that step here, while it does state it in the FP8 calculation.
root_cause: The +N−1 policy step is applied implicitly in the FP16 line but explicitly in the FP8 line, creating an apparent arithmetic gap.
correction: Either write '19.7 + 1 (N−1) = 20.7 → 21 hosts' or add a parenthetical: '(19.7 raw + 1 N−1 reserve → 21)'. Match the FP8 line's explicit '+N−1' phrasing.
acceptance_test: The FP16 peak-KV line shows the +N−1 step explicitly, and 19.7 + 1 = 20.7 → 21 is arithmetically visible.

quoted_clause: samples 1,000 retrievals per cycle (n ≈ 1,000 sized for the <0.3% target at 95% confidence; 0.001 resolution)
observed: With n=1,000 and a true rate near 0.3%, the expected event count is 3. The 95% binomial CI for 3/1,000 is roughly [0.06%, 0.88%], which is far wider than the 0.3% target. n=1,000 gives a 95% upper bound of 0.3% only in the zero-event case (rule of three: 3/1,000 = 0.003). The claim 'sized for the <0.3% target at 95% confidence' is therefore only true under a zero-failure observation, not in general.
evidence: For p=0.003, n=1,000: SE = sqrt(0.003×0.997/1,000) ≈ 0.00173; 95% CI half-width ≈ 0.0034. Zero-event 95% upper bound = 3/1,000 = 0.003. The '0.001 resolution' is the measurement granularity (1 event per 1,000), not the confidence-interval width.
root_cause: Conflating measurement granularity (0.001) with statistical confidence at the target rate.
correction: Rephrase: 'n ≈ 1,000 gives 0.001 measurement granularity and a 95% zero-event upper bound of 0.3%; detecting a true rate near 0.3% with a tight CI requires a larger n (e.g., ~3,000–4,000 for a ±0.1% half-width at p≈0.003).'
acceptance_test: The text distinguishes granularity from CI width and does not claim n=1,000 is sufficient to estimate a 0.3% rate with a tight 95% CI.

quoted_clause: However, two metrics remain above target: the false-positive rate at 2.4% ... and the guardrail-trigger rate at 5.4 per 1,000 (target <5); the poisoned-hit rate sits exactly at its ≈0.003 ceiling.
observed: The §4.1 table defines the poisoned-hit-rate target as '< 0.003'. A value of 0.003 is not < 0.003, so the poisoned-hit rate does not meet target. The mini-case counts only two metrics as 'above target' and treats the poisoned-hit rate as merely 'at its ceiling', implying it passes. Three metrics fail target at Cycle 2, not two.
evidence: Table 24-1 target column: 'Poisoned-hit rate | < 0.003'. Cycle 2 value: 0.003. 0.003 < 0.003 is false. The mini-case's own sentence says the rate 'sits exactly at its ≈0.003 ceiling' — i.e., at the boundary, not below it.
root_cause: Inconsistent treatment of the '<' operator: the table uses strict '<', but the mini-case prose treats 'at 0.003' as passing.
correction: Either (a) change the target to '≤ 0.003' in Table 24-1 and §4.1, or (b) rephrase the mini-case to say 'three metrics do not meet target: FP 2.4%, guardrail 5.4/1,000, and poisoned-hit 0.003 (at the <0.003 ceiling, not below it).'
acceptance_test: The mini-case and Table 24-1 agree on whether 0.003 meets the poisoned-hit target, and the count of failing metrics is consistent.

quoted_clause: per-request KV at 9.2K = 24.2 GB (2 × 80 layers × 9.2K × 8,192 × 2 B): KV, already inside the ~436 GB KV budget at concurrency (17 × ~24.9 GB ≈ 423 GB)
observed: The text computes per-request KV at 9.2K = 24.2 GB, then immediately uses 24.9 GB (the 9.5K figure) for the concurrency check. The switch from 24.2 to 24.9 is not explained. A reader may wonder whether the 24.2 GB or the 24.9 GB is the per-request KV.
evidence: 24.2 GB is at 9.2K input; 24.9 GB is at 9.5K total (9.2K input + 300 output). The concurrency check correctly uses the max KV (24.9 GB), but the text presents 24.2 GB first without flagging the switch.
root_cause: Two different context lengths (9.2K input vs 9.5K total) are used in adjacent sentences without an explicit transition.
correction: Add a clause: 'per-request KV at 9.2K input = 24.2 GB; at the 9.5K max (input + 300 output) it is 24.9 GB, which is the figure used for the concurrency check: 17 × 24.9 ≈ 423 GB.'
acceptance_test: The text explicitly distinguishes the 9.2K-input KV (24.2 GB) from the 9.5K-max KV (24.9 GB) and states which is used for the concurrency check.

quoted_clause: the miss value assumes that queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps (compute falls from the inflated 320 ms to ~120 ms, so 250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50)
observed: The 120 ms 'queue-drained' compute is asserted, not derived. At 1.3 rps against a ~2.0 req/s ceiling, ρ ≈ 0.65, so the queue is not fully drained; some queueing delay remains. The 120 ms figure is a scenario input, but the text presents it as if it follows from 'queue has drained'.
evidence: Utilization at 1.3 rps / 2.0 rps = 0.65. At ρ=0.65, an M/M/1 queue has mean wait = ρ/(1−ρ) × service time ≈ 1.86 × service time, which is not negligible. The 120 ms may be plausible as a service-plus-small-queue figure, but the text does not show the derivation.
root_cause: The 120 ms is a scenario input presented as a consequence of 'queue has drained', but at ρ=0.65 the queue is not fully drained.
correction: Either (a) label 120 ms explicitly as a scenario input ('we assume the queue-drained compute is ~120 ms; this is a Step 3 load-test target'), or (b) show the queueing calculation that yields 120 ms at ρ=0.65.
acceptance_test: The 120 ms figure is either derived from a stated queueing model or explicitly labeled as a scenario input, not presented as a consequence of 'queue has drained'.

issue: The token-1 box is labelled 'from prefill' and feeds directly into 'append K/V', which can be read as saying prefill writes token 1's K/V. The prose later establishes that token 1 is sampled at the end of prefill and its K/V is written only when token 1 is processed as input in the first decode step.
evidence: Figure 1.1 shows token1 'from prefill' → append K/V. Page 14 states: 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' The caption says 'written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled', but the diagram has no step boundary separating prefill from first decode.
acceptance_test: Either add a visible prefill/decode boundary and place token 1 on the decode side as the first decode input, or relabel token 1 as 'sampled at end of prefill; written on first decode step'. Verify a reader cannot infer that prefill appends token 1's K/V.

issue: The Token IDs box contains 'Integers order = position', which can be read as saying the integer token ID encodes or determines position. Token IDs are vocabulary indices; position is supplied separately by position IDs/positional encoding.
evidence: Figure 1.2: 'Token IDs / Integers / order = position'. The caption describes only 'text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV cache' and does not define or justify 'order = position'.
acceptance_test: Replace with 'integer vocabulary IDs; sequence order gives position' or add a separate position input. Verify the figure no longer implies that the token-ID value itself encodes position.

issue: The arrow from Embedding to Attention is labelled 'attend'. Embeddings do not attend; attention consumes the embedded token and computes Q/K/V. The label misassigns the attention operation to the embedding-to-attention transition.
evidence: Figure 1.2 shows 'Embedding' → 'attend' → 'Attention'. The Attention box itself says 'Q,K,V (this token) vs all past tokens'. The caption says 'embedding → attention', not that embedding performs attention.
acceptance_test: Relabel the arrow 'project to Q/K/V' or 'input embeddings'. Verify the word 'attend' appears only on the attention operation or the KV-cache read path, not on the embedding output.

issue: The diagram shows Attention → 'append K,V' → KV Cache, which suggests attention produces or appends K/V after computing attention. In the transformer, K/V for the current token are computed by projection before attention uses them; attention reads cached K/V and the current K/V, and the current K/V are stored for future steps.
evidence: Figure 1.2: 'Attention' box → arrow 'append K,V' → 'KV Cache'. The caption itself warns: 'The K/V are produced within every applicable layer (not after a single "attention" stage)'. The drawn causal order still places append after the Attention box.
acceptance_test: Redraw so current-token K/V are produced before or alongside attention, with attention reading past K/V from cache plus current K/V, and the append/store path clearly storing current K/V for future steps. Verify the figure no longer implies attention outputs K/V.

issue: The caption says the pipeline is 'in three bands' and then refers to 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box'. Visually there are two process bands (PREFILL and DECODE) plus one central cache box, not three bands plus a box.
evidence: Figure 2.1 has two labelled horizontal bands, 'PREFILL' and 'DECODE', and a separate central box labelled 'PERSISTENT KV CACHE'. Caption: 'in three bands' and 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings'.
acceptance_test: Change the caption to 'two process bands plus the persistent KV-cache box' or explicitly label the cache as the third band. Verify the caption's count matches the visual grouping.

issue: The drawn roofline is inconsistent with the stated H100 bandwidth. At arithmetic intensity 1 FLOP/byte, the black roofline intersects the left axis at about 1e12 FLOP/s, but 3.35 TB/s implies 3.35e12 FLOP/s. The drawn line therefore has a log-log slope of about 1.21 instead of 1, even though the caption and ridge label claim a 3.35 TB/s roofline with ridge at ~295 FLOP/byte.
evidence: Figure 2.2 caption: 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'. Roofline: attainable = min(989e12, AI × 3.35e12). At AI = 1, attainable = 3.35e12 FLOP/s, not 1e12. The drawn black line starts at approximately (1, 1e12) and reaches (295, 989e12), which is not the stated bandwidth slope.
acceptance_test: Recompute and redraw the memory-bound segment through (1, 3.35e12) and (295, 989e12); verify the log-log slope is 1 and the intercept matches 3.35 TB/s. Confirm the decode marker at ~1 FLOP/byte sits below the corrected roof, not below a too-low roof.

figure: Figure 3.4 — Dense vs MoE parameter allocation and KV cache behavior
issue: The red KV comparison callout is duplicated verbatim under both the Dense 70B and MoE columns: both read “dense 12 GB vs MoE 0.6 GB.” Because each callout sits inside a single model column, the layout implies that both columns contain the same two-value comparison rather than assigning 12 GB to the dense model and 0.6 GB to the MoE model. This is especially risky because the figure’s central claim is that the KV difference comes from attention shape, not MoE routing; the duplicated callout visually reinforces the opposite reading.
evidence: Rendered page shows two separate red boxes, one under the Dense 70B column and one under the MoE column, both containing the identical text “dense 12 GB vs MoE 0.6 GB.” The caption correctly states “~12 GB vs ~0.6 GB at 9.2K/8-bit” and “the gap is the shape, not the routing,” but the figure itself does not visually assign the values to the correct columns.
acceptance_test: Replace the two duplicated red callouts with either (a) one shared comparison callout spanning both columns, or (b) column-specific labels: “Dense KV ≈ 12 GB” under Dense 70B and “MoE KV ≈ 0.6 GB” under MoE, with a shared note that the difference is due to attention shape, not routing. Re-render and verify that a reader cannot infer that both models have both KV values.

figure: Figure 25.1 — Anatomy of an ADR, and how one ADR supersedes the next

figure: Figure 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes

figure: Figure A.1 — 2026 frontier MoE extreme sparsity
issue: The x-axis label says 'Active parameters as % of total', but the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next bar is explicitly computed against the 125B backbone only, excluding the 51B n-gram embedding and 4B MTP. The axis label therefore states a denominator that is false for one of the four plotted bars.

issue: The GLM KV-cache scope label is ambiguous and inconsistent with the caption: the table says 'BF16 / layer' under KV cache, while the caption says GLM rows are 'per-layer/per-head scope'. 'BF16' is a precision, not a scope, and 'per head' is missing from the KV label.

issue: The green model name and green italic scope annotations are low-contrast on white, especially at print size and in grayscale. 'GLM-5.3-Flash', 'BF16 / layer', and 'attention only per head / layer' are rendered in a light green that is difficult to read.

acceptance_test: Darken the green or use black/dark-gray text with a green marker; verify small-text contrast ≥4.5:1 and legibility in a grayscale print proof.

issue: The plotted p99 marker (1.33 s) visually contradicts the plotted 1% straggler mass at ~5 s. The caption says 'Successive state snapshots, not jointly retained history', but the diagram's layout works against that correction.

The caption explicitly says 'Successive state snapshots, not jointly retained history' and 'recurrent snapshots are successive, not jointly retained.' issue: The caption says 'The same 70B model serves in ~165 GB (weights + KV, max 9.5K — canonical input 9.2K)', but the bar is labeled 'Inference (weights+KV)' and the note says activation, microbatch/sequence, and offload/checkpointing are NOT included. Activation, microbatch/sequence, and offload/checkpointing are NOT included (Table 7-2).' Caption: 'The same 70B model serves in ~165 GB (weights + KV, max 9.5K — canonical input 9.2K) ...'
acceptance_test: Change the caption to say 'has a weights+KV floor of ~165 GB' rather than 'serves in ~165 GB', and ensure the bar label or caption explicitly says 'floor, not full deployment footprint'. The reader should not be able to infer that 165 GB is sufficient for a production serving configuration.

issue: The top-left box labels AWQ/GPTQ as an 'Error-control method'. AWQ and GPTQ are post-training quantization algorithms, not merely error-control methods. The label is defensible as a shorthand for calibration-guided error reduction, but it is less precise than the rest of the figure and may teach a misleading category.
evidence: Box text: 'Error-control method / AWQ / GPTQ / Calibration guides error reduction'. Caption: 'Quantization choices and execution paths: error-control method, numerical representation, packed tensors and checkpoint container describe different parts of a deployment...'
acceptance_test: Rename the box to 'Quantization method / calibration' or 'Scale/error calibration method' and keep AWQ/GPTQ as examples. The figure should distinguish quantization algorithm from numerical representation without implying AWQ/GPTQ are only error-control mechanisms.

issue: The KV band's request-slot boundaries are not visually distinguishable from the decorative dot fill. The caption says faint vertical rules mark the 24.9 GB request slots, but at print size the reader cannot count or see 17 full slots plus the half slot; the figure therefore does not visually support the concurrency arithmetic it is meant to explain.

The caption claims 'faint vertical rules inside the KV band mark those 24.9 GB request slots,' but the vertical dot columns blend into the horizontal dot rows. The equation below gives 17.5 slots, yet the bar does not visibly encode 17.5 divisions.
acceptance_test: Redraw the KV band with distinct, thin vertical slot boundaries (17 full slots plus one half-slot), remove or suppress the competing dot grid, and verify at 100% print size and in grayscale that a reader can count the slots and see the half-slot.

issue: The color legend contradicts the figure's central distinction. Shared memory, L2 cache, and registers are storage resources but are colored blue, which the legend labels 'compute.' Conversely, 'other GPUs / remote' is colored green, which the legend labels 'interconnect,' even though it denotes a remote device/resource rather than a link. The single vertical stack and red gradient arrow also reinforce a one-ladder reading that the caption explicitly denies.
evidence: Legend: blue = compute, orange = memory, green = interconnect. But 'shared mem (SRAM)' and 'L2 cache' are blue; 'registers' is blue; 'other GPUs / remote' is green. The caption says compute, memory, and interconnect are 'separate groups within this stack, not levels of one ladder,' yet the figure draws one continuous vertical stack with one red 'capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows' arrow spanning all categories.
acceptance_test: Recolor by resource type: compute units, on-chip memory, off-chip memory, interconnect, and remote device. Separate the groups visually (e.g., parallel columns or brackets) and restrict the gradient arrow to the memory hierarchy. Verify that the legend matches every box and that the figure remains interpretable in grayscale.

issue: The y-axis label 'Achievable performance' conflicts with the caption's statement that the ceilings are 'peak/theoretical datasheet values, not achieved rates.' A reader can reasonably read 'achievable' as measured or attainable in practice, which is exactly the misconception the caption tries to prevent.
evidence: Y-axis: 'Achievable performance (TFLOPS) — per GPU.' Caption: 'the ceilings are peak/theoretical datasheet values, not achieved rates (sustained MFU is 30–40%, §8.3).' The chart's plateau is a theoretical roofline bound, not an achieved rate.

issue: The legend says blue = data/state and orange = compute, but UMT5-XXL and VAE encode are compute modules and are colored blue. This makes the visual encoding inconsistent with the legend and obscures which boxes are computation versus data.
evidence: Legend: 'Blue: data/state. Orange: compute.' The 'UMT5-XXL ≤512 prompt tokens' box and the 'VAE encode I2V condition only' box are blue, although both are neural-network compute modules. By contrast, 'Wan2.2 dense TI2V-5B + scheduler' and 'VAE decode' are orange.
acceptance_test: Recolor UMT5-XXL and VAE encode as compute (orange), or introduce and label a third category such as 'conditioning encoder' with its own legend entry. Verify that every box's color matches its role and that the legend explains all colors used.

issue: The legend contains the sentence 'Token partitioning adds communication between devices,' but no visual symbol or annotation depicts token partitioning or inter-device communication. The legend is therefore carrying prose that does not explain any visual encoding.
evidence: Legend text: 'Solid: data/state flow. Dashed: denoiser conditioning. Blue: data/state. Orange: compute. Token partitioning adds communication between devices.' No box, arrow, or symbol in the diagram represents token partitioning or communication.
acceptance_test: Either add a visual symbol/annotation for token partitioning and inter-device communication, or move the sentence to the caption as a scope note. The legend should contain only keys that map to visible encodings.

figure: Figure 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue: The figure note says 'no offload, latency or overlap', but the plotted 544 ms value depends on concurrent send and receive (overlap of the two directions). The note can therefore be read as contradicting the model used to produce the curve.
evidence: Caption: 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount. Curves use 450 GB/s ...'. Prose on printed p. 156: 'With concurrent send and receive, its ideal time is T_ring ≈ 245/450 ≈ 0.54 s. Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time.' Figure note: 'Analytical model; no offload, latency or overlap; not measured.' If 'overlap' meant no send/receive overlap, the time would be 490/450 ≈ 1.09 s, not 0.54 s.
acceptance_test: Revise the note to say 'no offload, latency, or communication/computation overlap' (or equivalent), so it cannot be read as denying the concurrent send/receive assumption behind the plotted times.

figure: Figure 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue: The caption does not state the time formula used for the curves. A reader can see 'sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes' and 'ideal ring completion time' but is not told that the plotted time is sent bytes per rank divided by directional bandwidth, with send and receive concurrent.
evidence: Subtitle: 'sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes'. Caption: 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount. Curves use 450 GB/s ...'. The caption never says 'time = sent bytes per rank / directional bandwidth' or 'assuming concurrent send and receive'. The prose on p. 156 supplies this, but the figure caption should be self-contained.
acceptance_test: Add one clause to the caption: 'Plotted time is sent bytes per rank divided by directional bandwidth, assuming concurrent send and receive.'

issue: The figure says 'Balanced ring neighbor order (both phases)' and shows R0→R1→R2→R3→R0, but it does not show which 2 B chunk each rank sends in each round. For a reader trying to reconstruct the ring algorithm, the diagram shows the neighbor order but not the chunk rotation that makes reduce-scatter and all-gather work.
evidence: Figure text: 'Balanced ring neighbor order (both phases)' with R0→R1→R2→R3→R0. Below: 'Each round sends one 2 B chunk to the next rank.' The figure does not label the chunks (e.g., chunk 0, chunk 1, chunk 2, chunk 3) or show which chunk moves in round 1, 2, 3. The caption says 'Reduce-scatter leaves one reduced element per rank; all-gather then replicates the already-reduced fragments', but the chunk rotation is left implicit.
acceptance_test: Either add small chunk labels (0/1/2/3) to the ring arrows or add one sentence to the caption: 'In round r, rank i sends chunk (i−r) mod N; the same rotation is used in both phases.'

figure: Figure 9.3 — The payload path is not the bootstrap path
issue: The figure's right-hand path places 'Plugin: MPI or OFI' under '3 Device runtime plus transport', while the bottom note says 'GPU-aware MPI can carry payload too; MPI is not CPU-only.' The diagram therefore shows MPI in two different roles (setup/control and transport/plugin) without visually distinguishing those roles.

Right path under '3 Device runtime plus transport': 'SYCL / Level Zero path / Plugin: MPI or OFI / Actual path depends on build'. Caption: 'Dashed setup connections do not imply that MPI carries the collective payload; GPU-aware MPI is also a possible payload implementation.' The figure uses the same word 'MPI' for setup and for a possible transport/plugin without a visual or textual role distinction.
acceptance_test: Either label the right-path MPI entry as 'MPI transport (payload-capable)' or add a caption sentence: 'MPI appears in two roles: setup/rendezvous (dashed) and, in some builds, payload transport (solid); the figure does not imply they are the same path.'

issue: Panel B's pipeline-bubble annotation is a text line flush against the panel's left border and no bubble region is drawn; the caption says the panel shows 'an idle bubble at fill/drain'.
evidence: The line 'idle (bubble) at fill/drain — pipeline-wide' begins at the panel border (first glyph at the border, no inset) and sits below three GPU boxes with no shaded or dashed idle region. acceptance_test: Redraw panel B with a visible bubble region (e.g., dashed idle slots at pipeline fill/drain) and inset the annotation by at least one text-height from the panel border; verify at print size that no glyph is clipped and that the bubble is visually distinguishable from the stage boxes.

issue: The all-reduce arrow originates only from GPU 0, while the label says 'all-reduce partial sums'; the figure does not show GPU 1 contributing to the collective.

acceptance_test: Add a second arrow from GPU 1 to the all-reduce box, or draw a bidirectional/collective arrow between both GPUs and the box; verify the visual is symmetric and matches the all-reduce semantics.

issue: The legend defines green as 'new sequence (backfill)', but the right panel draws green as thin vertical bars between blue segments; the new sequence then continues as blue. This makes green look like an instantaneous admission marker, not a sequence with duration.

issue: The caption 'Table 11-1 — Serving techniques at a glance' is stranded at the bottom of the page with no table content; the table begins on the following page.

issue: Panel A shows four prefill GPUs and four decode GPUs but a single KV arrow labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'; the caveat compares aggregate 1.4 TB/s to 'any single link above' without noting the four-link aggregate (4 × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s). The figure therefore invites the false inference that the green total curve crosses the red linear curve at ~106.8K.

The green curve in the figure follows the red linear curve at low L and remains above it at high L; it does not cross it.
acceptance_test: Either (a) add a separate dashed curve for the causal-triangle quadratic term and point the 'crossover ~106.8K' annotation at its intersection with the red linear curve, or (b) relabel the annotation to make clear that it marks where the causal-triangle quadratic component equals the linear term, not where the green total curve crosses linear. page_hint: Ch 4, §3 Worked Example (memory planning paragraph) and §8 Mini-Case and §7 What We Still Don't Know
quoted_clause: 436 GB ÷ 24.1 GB ≈ 18" (memory planning) vs "C ≈ 17.5 is the analytical quotient, floored to 17 deployable whole-context slots per the book's whole-slot convention, Chapters 14/16/17" (mini-case) vs "a single 8×H100 host holds ~17.5 KV-resident requests (the conservative integer floor is 17)" (What We Still Don't Know)"
observed: The in-chapter arithmetic 436 GB / 24.1 GB = 18.09 ≈ 18, but the same chapter uses C ≈ 17.5 (floored to 17) for fleet sizing. The 17.5 is attributed to 'Chapters 14/16/17' without explaining why it differs from the local 436/24.1 calculation. This changes the host count: 86/17 = 5.06 → 6 hosts (as printed) vs 86/18 = 4.78 → 5 hosts. Similarly 344/17 = 20.24 → 21 vs 344/18 = 19.1 → 20.
evidence: 436 / 24.1 = 18.09. The text explicitly writes '436 GB ÷ 24.1 GB ≈ 18' in the memory planning paragraph. Three other locations in the same chapter use 17.5/17. The 17.5 is not derived from any numbers stated in Ch 4; it is imported from later chapters without a bridging explanation. If the later chapters use a different available-KV figure (e.g., 422 GB with 78 GB workspace) or a different per-request KV (e.g., 25 GB rounded up), that is not stated here.
root_cause: The canonical KV-slot count is computed in Ch 14/16/17 with additional constraints (possibly a larger workspace reservation or a rounded-up per-request KV) that yield 17.5, but Ch 4 presents the local arithmetic (436/24.1 ≈ 18) without reconciling it to the 17.5 used for fleet sizing in the same chapter. The reader doing the math gets 18, not 17.5.
correction: Either (a) change the memory-planning sentence to '436 GB ÷ 24.1 GB ≈ 18 (the fleet-sizing chapters refine this to 17.5 with additional per-rank overhead; see Ch 14/16/17)', or (b) if the 17.5 is the correct canonical figure, adjust the local arithmetic to show the additional constraint that reduces 18.09 to 17.5 (e.g., a 78 GB workspace instead of 64 GB, or a 25 GB per-request KV). The host counts (6/21) must be consistent with whichever slot count is used.
acceptance_test:
A reader who computes 436/24.1 from the stated numbers in Ch 4 arrives at the same integer slot count (17 or 18) that the mini-case and fleet-sizing paragraphs use. No unexplained gap between the local arithmetic and the imported 17.5."

page_hint: Ch 4, §3 Worked Example, 'Economic Constraints' paragraph and the 'Cost-basis distinction' table
quoted_clause: The dollar denominator must be the whole fleet that serves this rate, not one host. At the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour (≈ $0.0333 per second), so ~92,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~2.76 million input tokens per cloud dollar and ~3,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~90,000 output tokens per cloud dollar.
observed: The economic paragraph interleaves at least five distinct cost bases (per-token API price, whole-fleet $/hr, single-host planning rate, per-request API cost, per-request owned-fleet cost) in a single dense block with multiple parenthetical qualifications. A reader must hold all five in working memory to avoid conflating them. The 'Cost-basis distinction' table helps but appears after the dense prose, and the table itself contains a very long cell for the self-host row.
evidence: The paragraph contains: (1) $1.20/$2.00 per 1M API price, (2) $120/hr whole-fleet, (3) 2.76M/90K tokens per cloud dollar, (4) 19,800 tok/s single-host planning rate, (5) 3.56M prefill tokens per host-dollar, (6) $0.012 per request API basis, (7) $0.0033/$0.0029 per request owned-fleet basis, (8) $0.00056 dimensionally-wrong figure, (9) $0.362/$11.11/$0.3509 per 1M normalizations. Nine distinct numbers in one paragraph.
root_cause: The section tries to establish the cost framework, prevent a specific conflation (single-host vs whole-fleet), and provide the canonical numbers all at once. The pedagogical goal is clear but the delivery is a single dense block rather than a progressive build.
correction: Split into three shorter sub-paragraphs: (1) 'The two cost bases' (API per-token vs owned-fleet $/hr), (2) 'The whole-fleet tokens-per-dollar' (with the 2.76M/90K figures and the single-host 3.56M contrast), (3) 'Per-request cost on each basis' ($0.012 API vs $0.0033/$0.0029 owned). Move the 'Cost-basis distinction' table before the prose that references it, or make it the primary presentation with the prose as annotation. The dimensionally-wrong $0.00056 example can be a single sentence in a footnote or parenthetical rather than inline.
acceptance_test:
A reader can identify the two cost bases and the three tokens-per-dollar figures without re-reading the paragraph more than once. No single sentence contains more than two distinct cost figures."
  }

quoted_clause: or in worst cases a fragment of a character
observed: The phrase 'a fragment of a character' is technically correct (a single byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 codepoint) but may lead a reader to think the tokenizer splits individual characters into sub-character pieces. The subsequent BPE description ('byte-pair encoding (BPE) repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent byte/subword pairs') clarifies the byte-level operation, but the initial list of token types could be more precise.
evidence: BPE operates on bytes. A 'token' in the worst case is a single byte, which for a multi-byte UTF-8 character (e.g., a 4-byte emoji) is indeed a fragment of that character. But the phrasing 'fragment of a character' without the byte-level qualifier could be misread as 'a piece of a letter' in a character-level sense.
root_cause: The list is written from the reader's perspective (what the token looks like) rather than the implementation perspective (what the tokenizer produces). The byte-level mechanism is explained two sentences later.
correction: Change to 'or in worst cases a single byte (which for multi-byte Unicode characters is a fragment of a character)'. This preserves the reader-facing intuition while anchoring it to the byte-level mechanism that the BPE description will elaborate.
acceptance_test:
A reader who stops after the first sentence and does not read the BPE paragraph still understands that the worst-case token is a byte, not an arbitrary sub-character slice."
  }

page_hint: Ch 3, §1 Concept, 'Alternative inference' subsection (from 'From corruption to learned generation' through 'State reuse follows dependency boundaries')

It is the book's coverage of the 2026 alternative-inference frontier; the core dense/MoE/KV thread resumes in §2 (Mental Model).

While the 'Reader orientation' note tells the reader they can skip, the section's length and density create a significant interruption to the main thread. A reader who does not skip must hold the diffusion material in working memory while also tracking the dense/MoE argument that resumes in §2.
evidence: The section covers: continuous denoising diffusion, score-based SDEs, discrete diffusion (MDLM, LLaDA), flow matching, rectified flow, masked language sampling, parallel prediction, agent-loop distinction, state reuse under bidirectional attention, block-causal models, DiffusionGemma, LLaDA2.2, and Wan2.2 A14B. That is at least 8 distinct technical topics in one subsection.
root_cause: The book wants to cover the 2026 alternative-inference frontier without creating a separate chapter (which would break the token→fleet spine). Placing it in Ch 3 (model understanding) is the right location, but the delivery as a single continuous subsection is too dense for the main reading path.
correction: Add a 3–4 sentence summary at the end of the section that states the key architectural consequence for the main thread (e.g., 'The one point that carries forward: in diffusion/alternative inference, the execution unit is a model evaluation over a canvas, not a token; the total-vs-active and KV-residency frameworks of this chapter still apply, but the per-token accounting must be replaced by per-evaluation accounting. The full treatment is Ch 27 and Appendix A.'). This gives the non-skipping reader a clean exit point and a bridge back to the main thread without requiring them to hold all 8 topics in memory.
acceptance_test:
A reader who finishes the alternative-inference section can state in one sentence what it means for the dense/MoE framework before reading §2. The section has a clear 'so what for the main thread' conclusion."

page_hint: Ch 2, §2 Mental Model, prefill/decode water metaphor
quoted_clause: It is like pushing the water of that same 140 GB reservoir through a standard garden hose: the whole volume must flow every 25 milliseconds just to deliver one glass of water — one generated token.
observed: The metaphor frames the 140 GB as a 'reservoir' of water that must be pushed through a hose. In the actual mechanism, the 140 GB is the weight matrix stored in HBM, and the 'hose' is the HBM-to-SM data path. The metaphor is effective for the bandwidth-bound intuition, but 'reservoir' subtly implies a volume of fluid being consumed, whereas the weights are re-read (not consumed) every step. A careful reader might wonder whether the 140 GB is 'used up' after one token.
evidence: The text immediately after the metaphor says 'the pump (compute) is more than powerful enough, but the diameter of the hose (HBM bandwidth) physically cannot move that volume of water in that time frame.' The 'move that volume' phrasing is correct (the data is moved, not consumed). But 'reservoir' + 'pushing the water' could imply consumption.
root_cause: The water metaphor is a standard and effective analogy for bandwidth-bound vs compute-bound. The 'reservoir' framing is a minor imprecision in an otherwise clear analogy.
correction: Optional: change 'pushing the water of that same 140 GB reservoir through a standard garden hose' to 'streaming the full 140 GB of weight data through a standard garden hose (HBM bandwidth) every 25 milliseconds'. This removes the 'reservoir' (implies a tank being drained) and makes the re-read nature explicit. Alternatively, add a half-sentence: 'The reservoir is not drained — the same 140 GB is re-read every step, but the hose is too narrow to move it in 25 ms.'

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a), the [HYPOTHESIS] paragraph beginning 'for the canonical 2,000-user workload'
quoted_clause: the incremental per-request compute cost of the 768-dim (all-mpnet) vs 384-dim (MiniLM) embedding models — a cross-model difference, not a dim-only sweep — is ~11.1 GFLOP per 64-token query (2 × params × L: 14.08 − 2.94 GFLOP, the §3(a) embedding table's own rows; a same-family 384-dim variant halves index storage (encoder compute ~unchanged)) — ~56–370 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at a realistic 30–200 GFLOP/s, but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU, which is the basis the ~120 ms retrieval budget already assumes (vector search and reranking on a local GPU, Ch 4). On that basis the incremental cost stays well within the ~120 ms retrieval budget; single-core encoding fits only at the high end of that throughput range (55.5 ms at 200 GFLOP/s vs 370 ms at 30 GFLOP/s) — conditional on measured single-core throughput. The decision hinges on whether the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain (an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS], domain- and corpus-specific — §5.3) translates into sufficient answer-quality improvement to justify the ~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64-token query, Table 5-1) — a workload-specific tradeoff, not a universal rule.
observed: A single ~200-word paragraph embeds six distinct calculations (FLOP delta, CPU time range, GPU time, budget comparison, single-core throughput range, MAP-vs-FLOP tradeoff) with nested parentheticals and cross-references. The reader must hold all intermediate values in working memory to follow the argument. The paragraph's intellectual job is to show that the 768-dim choice is compute-justified and that the quality claim remains unvalidated, but the density obscures both points.
evidence: All individual numbers are arithmetically correct (14.08−2.94=11.14≈11.1; 11.1/200=55.5 ms; 11.1/30=370 ms; 11.1/10000=1.11 ms; 14.08/2.94≈4.8×). The problem is presentation, not correctness.
root_cause: The paragraph attempts to do the full quantitative comparison and the qualitative recommendation in one block, without separating the computation from the decision logic.
correction: Split into two or three shorter paragraphs: (1) the FLOP delta and its time implications on CPU vs GPU (a short table or 2–3 sentences); (2) the budget comparison (one sentence: 'on the GPU basis the ~1.1 ms incremental cost is negligible against the 120 ms retrieval budget'); (3) the decision logic (the MAP-vs-FLOP tradeoff, with the [HYPOTHESIS] label on the MAP claim). This preserves all content while reducing cognitive load.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the three distinct intellectual moves (compute cost, budget fit, quality tradeoff) without re-reading the paragraph more than once.

page_hint: Ch 5, §1, 'Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict'
quoted_clause: Parallel refinement (diffusion-style decoding that updates many token positions per step) is worth investigating when low-batch latency or constrained infilling dominates, but neither advantage follows from a model-family label. AR fill-in-the-middle (FIM) models — autoregressive models trained to infill a marked span — are a necessary editing baseline.

The section's connection to the chapter's main argument (workload-driven model selection for the canonical RAG system) is not made explicit. A reader may wonder why these modes are relevant to an enterprise Q&A RAG tool. The section also introduces the term 'infilling' without defining it in the context of the canonical workload.

The section's last sentence ('The selection question is whether the specific model, sampler and runtime meet the workload's quality, output and SLO requirements together') is a general principle that applies to AR as well.

For workloads that might use non-AR generation (editing, infilling, image-to-text), the mode itself becomes an additional selection dimension.' page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Latency Is a Distribution, Not a Mean' — the p99 explanation
quoted_clause: a knife-edge property of this N = 10,000 sample, not of the distribution: linear interpolation lands on the largest non-straggler draw, while the population p99 of the stated 99% log-normal + 1% straggler mixture is 5.0 s (one extra straggler, 101 of 10,000, moves the sample p99 to 5.0 s too)
observed: The explanation of why the sample p99 is 1.33 s while the population p99 is 5.0 s is technically correct but requires the reader to hold in mind: (a) the sample composition (9,900 log-normal + 100 stragglers), (b) the linear-interpolation method for percentiles, (c) the CDF jump at 5.0 s in the population, and (d) the sensitivity to one extra straggler. The 'knife-edge' framing is apt but the mechanism is not made concrete enough for a first reading. A reader who is not already fluent in order-statistic interpolation may accept the conclusion without understanding why.
evidence: The math is correct: with 10,000 samples, p99 is at rank 9,901 (1-indexed). The 9,900th value is the max log-normal draw (~1.33 s); the 9,901st is a straggler at 5.0 s. Linear interpolation between ranks 9,900 and 9,901 at the 0.99 quantile gives a value between 1.33 and 5.0, but the text says p99 ≈ 1.33, which corresponds to the 9,900th order statistic (the 'largest non-straggler draw'). The population CDF jumps from 0.99 to 1.0 at 5.0, so the population p99 (smallest x with CDF(x)≥0.99) is 5.0. The 'one extra straggler' sensitivity is correct: with 101 stragglers, the 9,901st value is still a straggler, and the interpolated p99 moves toward 5.0.
root_cause: The explanation prioritizes the conceptual point (sample vs population percentile) over the mechanical point (how linear interpolation on a sorted sample produces the specific value 1.33).
correction: Add a one-sentence mechanical clarification: 'In the sorted sample, the 9,900th value is the largest log-normal draw (~1.33 s) and the 9,901st is the first straggler (5.0 s); the 0.99 quantile falls at rank 9,901, but standard linear interpolation between the 9,900th and 9,901st order statistics at the 0.9999 position yields a value near the 9,900th draw.' Alternatively, add a 3-row mini-table: rank 9,900 → 1.33 s; rank 9,901 → 5.0 s; population p99 → 5.0 s (CDF jump). This makes the knife-edge concrete without adding a full paragraph.
acceptance_test: A reader can explain to a colleague why the sample p99 is 1.33 s but the population p99 is 5.0 s, using the order-statistic mechanism, not just the 'knife-edge' label.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a), 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'

evidence: The sentence continues: 'its quality gain over all-mpnet-base-v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics), and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64-token embedding in the table above, the same ratio as their parameter counts) — validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it.' The quantitative argument is complete without 'overkill.'

page_hint: Ch 8, §6, 'From video dimensions to repeated attention work' — the Wan2.2 TI2V-5B worked example
quoted_clause: A worked example makes the new work unit concrete. We use Wan2.2 TI2V-5B in its text-to-video path, not the A14B expert model. Its configuration specifies a dense transformer with hidden width 3,072, 30 layers, and 24 attention heads. The VAE has 48 latent channels and temporal/spatial strides of 4, 16, and 16. The denoiser patches the latent video by (1,2,2). The release's '720P' example is precisely 1,280 × 704 pixels, 121 frames, at 24 frames/s. The dimensions, rather than the marketing resolution label, determine the budget.
observed: The Wan2.2 example is ~800 words of dense arithmetic spanning geometry (latent dimensions, patching), FLOP counting (attention core, per-layer, per-branch, total trajectory), memory (hidden tensor, score tensor), and sensitivity (frame count, spatial scaling). While every number is correct, the example introduces 15+ new quantities (T_l, H_l, W_l, N, d, C_attention, branch count, timestep count, BF16 hidden size, score tensor size, frame-to-second conversion) in a single continuous block. A reader who loses the thread at any point must re-read the entire section. The example's intellectual job is to show that 'fewer sequential evaluations can mean more total work' (the §1 principle) in a non-AR context, but the density obscures that connection.
evidence: All calculations verified: T_l=31, H_l=44, W_l=80, N=27,280, C_attention=9.145 TFLOP/layer, 274.341 TFLOP/branch, 27.434 PFLOP total, 167,608,320 B hidden, 35,721,523,200 B score, 33.268 GiB, 1.968× token scaling, 3.872× pairwise scaling, 5.0417 s. The example is arithmetically sound but pedagogically dense.
root_cause: The example was written to be comprehensive (covering geometry, FLOPs, memory, and sensitivity) rather than to illustrate one specific principle with minimal supporting detail.
correction: Restructure with explicit sub-steps: (1) 'Geometry: from pixels to tokens' (T_l, H_l, W_l, N — 4 lines); (2) 'Attention FLOPs per evaluation' (C_attention formula, per-layer, per-branch — 4 lines); (3) 'Total trajectory work' (branch count, timesteps, total PFLOP — 3 lines); (4) 'Memory boundary' (hidden tensor, score tensor, FlashAttention note — 4 lines); (5) 'Sensitivity' (frame scaling, spatial scaling, time convention — 4 lines). Add a one-sentence bridge at the start: 'This example applies the §1 principle (fewer sequential evaluations ≠ less total work) to a whole-clip denoiser, where 50 timesteps × 2 CFG branches = 100 evaluations each process all 27,280 tokens simultaneously.' The sensitivity and memory sections could be moved to a 'Further detail' sub-paragraph or a sidebar if the main text's purpose is the FLOP-counting principle.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the example's single main point (100 evaluations × 27,280 tokens = large total work despite few sequential steps) within 30 seconds of starting the section, without needing to follow all 15+ intermediate quantities.

page_hint: Ch 7, Fig 7.7 caption and the 'Technical note — per-rank fit' paragraph
quoted_clause: the 140 GB of weights shard to ~17.5 GB per GPU; the ~64 GB runtime/NCCL reserve is per-host (not per-rank); the ~436 GB KV budget shards to ~54.5 GB per GPU; and under tensor-parallel attention the per-request KV (24.9 GB) also shards across the 8 ranks, so the per-rank KV per request is ~3.1 GB. The 17.5 concurrent figure is therefore the aggregate bound — a rank can be the binding constraint even when the aggregate fits

However, the paragraph is dense with five distinct per-rank quantities in a single sentence, and the key insight (aggregate fit ≠ per-rank fit) is stated at the end after the reader has already processed all the numbers. The 'Technical note' label suggests it is supplementary, but it contains the most architecturally important caveat in the figure's context.
evidence: 140/8 = 17.5 ✓; 436/8 = 54.5 ✓; 24.9/8 = 3.1125 ≈ 3.1 ✓; 17.5 + 3.1 = 20.6 GB per rank for one request's weights + KV, well within 80 GB per rank. The aggregate 17.5 concurrent is correct; per-rank, 17.5 requests × 3.1 GB = 54.25 GB KV + 17.5 GB weights = 71.75 GB per rank, leaving 8.25 GB for runtime — tight but the text correctly says 'per-rank fit and sharding must be validated separately.'
root_cause: The per-rank breakdown was added as a clarification to the aggregate figure but was written as a single dense sentence rather than a structured list.
correction: Present the per-rank quantities as a short list or 2×3 table: (weights/rank: 17.5 GB; runtime/rank: 8 GB [64/8]; KV/rank per request: 3.1 GB; total per rank at 17.5 concurrent: 17.5 + 8 + 54.25 = 79.75 GB ≈ 80 GB). Then state the insight: 'At 17.5 concurrent requests, per-rank utilization reaches ~99.7% of the 80 GB rank capacity, leaving no room for fragmentation or workspace growth. The aggregate 17.5 is therefore a hard ceiling, not a comfortable operating point.' This makes the caveat concrete and actionable.
acceptance_test: A reader can see the per-rank budget at the 17.5-concurrent point and understand why it is a ceiling rather than a comfortable target, without re-deriving the five quantities from the prose.

page_hint: Ch 5, §2, 'Mental Model' — the input-heavy vs output-heavy paragraph
quoted_clause: If the workload is input-heavy (9.2K average input, 300-token output, ~30× more input than output), the system is first-order memory-capacity-bound (KV residency at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs — a first-order tendency to verify per workload, not a consequence of input-heaviness alone. If the workload were output-heavy, the token/FLOP mix shifts toward decode, which often makes decode bandwidth or latency critical — the actual bottleneck must be measured on the target stack.

However, the phrase 'memory-capacity-bound' is used without the full three-bound distinction that Ch 8 §1 establishes (compute-bound vs memory-bandwidth-bound vs memory-capacity-constrained). A reader encountering this in Ch 5 (before Ch 8) may conflate 'memory-capacity-bound' with 'memory-bandwidth-bound.' The Ch 8 distinction is the correct one, but Ch 5 uses the term before it is defined.

Memory-capacity-constrained (often KV-capacity-constrained in long-context inference) means feasible concurrency or context is limited by how much data fits in HBM.' Ch 5's 'memory-capacity-bound' matches the third definition but the reader has not yet seen the distinction.
root_cause: Ch 5 uses a term that is precisely defined in Ch 8, creating a forward-dependency on a distinction the reader has not yet learned.

Option (b) is simpler and avoids the forward reference.
acceptance_test: A reader who has not yet read Ch 8 can distinguish the 'memory-capacity' constraint (how many requests fit) from a 'memory-bandwidth' constraint (how fast each token is produced) based on Ch 5's text alone.

page_hint: Ch 7, §1, 'Count state by lifetime, not by the model label' — the 256-position canvas example
quoted_clause: As a shape-only example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary needs 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456 bytes, or 256 MiB, for one FP32 logits tensor at batch one. This excludes probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers and the rest of the model. It is not a measured model footprint.

evidence: 256 × 262,144 = 67,108,864; × 4 = 268,435,456 B = 256 MiB. ✓. The point is that a single intermediate tensor (logits for 256 positions) can be 256 MiB, which is non-trivial relative to a 24 GB device's budget, and that this tensor is not part of the AR KV cache formula.
root_cause: The example was written as a shape calculation without a preceding sentence stating the architectural point it illustrates.

For example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary produces a single FP32 logits tensor of 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 256 MiB at batch one — a non-trivial fraction of a 24 GB device's budget, and a cost the AR formula does not capture. This excludes the remaining model state (probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers, weights).'
acceptance_test: A reader can state in one sentence why the 256 MiB figure matters for the 'count state by lifetime' principle, without re-reading the paragraph.

page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Detecting the Regime' — the decode bandwidth paragraph
quoted_clause: Within a ~25 ms TPOT budget that demands 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s (batch-1-equivalent) of HBM bandwidth, against an H100's ~3.35 TB/s peak [1P][FACT]. Scope warning: this 5.6-vs-3.35 TB/s comparison is an illustrative single-device roofline argument, not the canonical 8×H100 host's actual deployment verdict.

The two scope notes (single-device vs 8×H100; aggregate vs per-rank) are then stated in a dense paragraph. The key insight (decode is bandwidth-bound because of low arithmetic intensity, not because 5.6 > 3.35) is buried at the end of the paragraph.
evidence: The 5.6 TB/s is the aggregate model-wide weight-read rate for a hypothetical single-device implementation. Under TP=8, each GPU reads 140/8 = 17.5 GB per token, requiring 17.5/0.025 = 0.7 TB/s against its 3.35 TB/s — well within capacity. The bandwidth-bound classification follows from the 1.0 FLOP/byte intensity (far below the 295 ridge), not from the 5.6 > 3.35 comparison. The text states all this correctly but in an order that risks the reader anchoring on the 5.6-vs-3.35 number first.
root_cause: The paragraph was structured as 'calculation → comparison → scope warning → deeper reason,' but the pedagogically effective order is 'deeper reason (intensity) → calculation (for illustration) → scope (why the calculation is not the verdict).'
correction: Restructure: (1) State the intensity argument first: 'Decode at batch 1 has an arithmetic intensity of ~1.0 FLOP/byte (140 GFLOP / 140 GB), far below the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge — this is why decode is bandwidth-bound, regardless of how many GPUs are used.' (2) Then give the single-device illustration: 'As a concrete single-device illustration: 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s exceeds one H100's 3.35 TB/s peak. Under TP=8, each GPU reads only 17.5 GB (0.7 TB/s), so the per-GPU bandwidth is not the binding constraint — the low intensity is.' (3) Then the scope note: 'This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch, decode intensity rises and can approach the ridge.'
