evidence: Printed p. 411: 'locate the dominant constraint: tail latency/queueing under the p99 ≈ 80 ms TTFT target'. Printed p. 414: 'under the hit-50 ms / miss-250 ms model p99 = 250 ms'. No sentence on either page states target met / not met.
acceptance_test: Add an explicit verdict to the mini-case (met / partially met / not met, with the residual gap and the next lever — e.g., inference sharding), and reflect that verdict in Fig 26.2's 'validate' step so the loop's exit condition is visible.

issue: The in-figure title ('Anatomy of an ADR, and how one ADR supersedes the next') restates the caption almost verbatim, and the two differ in wording ('ADR' vs 'Architecture Decision Record'), so the reader reads the same sentence twice and the caption contributes no interpretive content beyond the warning.
evidence: Rendered page: bold centered title above the diagram; caption below begins 'FIGURE 25.1: The Anatomy of an Architecture Decision Record, and how one ADR supersedes the next.'
acceptance_test: Delete the in-figure title and let the caption carry it, or replace the in-figure title with a one-line statement of the takeaway (e.g., 'A new ADR absorbs the old ADR's consequences as context; the old ADR is kept, not edited'). Acceptance: no sentence appears twice in near-identical form.

issue: Field-box text is set very small relative to the page: each of the five boxes carries a bold field name plus an italic gloss in a box roughly 0.25 in tall. The italic glosses ('the record', 'the situation', 'the choice', 'the effects', 'the rejected options') are the smallest text on the page and are the part of the figure that carries the caption's definitional content.
evidence: Rendered page at 150 dpi: each field box is ~18 px tall (~0.26 in) holding two lines of text; the italic gloss line is visibly smaller than the caption body type.
acceptance_test: Measure the rendered glyph sizes for the field names and glosses; raise any below 8 pt to ≥8 pt (gloss ≥8.5 pt italic), then re-render and confirm the five boxes still fit the card width without wrapping.

issue: Composition is left-heavy: the five field boxes occupy roughly the left fifth of each ADR card, leaving about three quarters of both cards empty, while the card headers are centered and the inter-record label floats in the resulting void. The reading order (centered header → far-left boxes) is not obvious, and the empty right half reads as unfinished rather than as deliberate whitespace.
evidence: Rendered page: field boxes span x≈90–175 of a ~415 px text block; the red label text sits at x≈205–330 with nothing to its right; both cards' rules span the full text width.
acceptance_test: Either widen the field boxes to fill the card (or lay the five fields out as a horizontal row within each card), or reduce the card width to the content and center the whole figure. Acceptance: the eye enters at the header and reaches the fields without a lateral jump, and no region of the figure is empty for more than one field-box width.

issue: The 'Traffic (rps)' category label attaches a physical unit to an axis whose values are authored 0–1 intensities. A reader glancing at the chart can read the bar heights as rps, which is the single most likely misreading of this figure.
evidence: Rendered page: x tick 'Traffic (rps)'; y axis 'Authored intensity (0–1)'; note 'per-axis 0–1 scale: compare within an axis, not across axes.'
acceptance_test: Change the tick label to 'Traffic volume' (or 'Traffic (rps) → intensity'), and confirm no other axis label carries a unit the 0–1 scale does not express.

issue: The in-figure title carries a design-process parenthetical — 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (grouped bars, not radar)' — that tells the reader about a chart type not used, and it duplicates the caption's subject rather than adding the takeaway.
evidence: Rendered page: chart title 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (grouped bars, not radar)'; caption 'FIGURE 26.1: Workload fingerprints on the six axes.'
acceptance_test: Remove '(grouped bars, not radar)' from the in-figure title; if the in-figure title is retained, make it state the takeaway (e.g., 'Each family peaks on a different axis') rather than restating the caption.

issue: Axis tick labels, category labels, legend entries and the italic note are all set smaller than the caption body type. The note ('per-axis 0–1 scale: compare within an axis, not across axes.') is the smallest text in the figure and carries the figure's most important interpretive caveat — the one that prevents the reader from comparing bar heights across axes.
evidence: Rendered page at 150 dpi: note text is visibly smaller than the caption's first line; tick labels ('0.0'…'1.0') are smaller than the legend text.
acceptance_test: Measure rendered sizes; bring all in-figure text to ≥8 pt (note ≥8.5 pt) and re-render; confirm the chart still fits the text block and the note remains on one line.

issue: The figure sits alone on a float page with roughly the top quarter and bottom quarter empty, and the chart itself is small relative to the text block. This under-fill is the direct cause of the sub-8 pt type noted above, and it separates the figure from the §26.2.1 matrix it visualizes.
evidence: Rendered page: running header at top, then blank space until the chart title at roughly 30% of page height; caption ends at roughly 70%.
acceptance_test: Enlarge the chart (taller plot area, larger fonts) to fill the text block, or move the figure onto the page carrying the §26.2.1 matrix so the reader can compare matrix rows and fingerprints side by side.

issue: The loop is drawn without the target that motivates it. The mini-case's constraint is a p99 TTFT target of ~80 ms, but neither the figure nor its caption shows it, so the diagram presents a loop that closes on itself with no criterion against which 'validate' can be performed.
evidence: Printed p. 411: 'tail latency/queueing under the p99 ≈ 80 ms TTFT target'. Printed p. 415 figure: box 1 'scenario TTFT p99 ~450 ms'; no 80 ms target appears anywhere in the figure or caption.
acceptance_test: Add the target to box 1 (e.g., 'scenario TTFT p99 ~450 ms vs ~80 ms target') or as a labelled target marker on the 'validate' arrow, and confirm the caption explains what 'validate' compares against.

issue: Box 3, the PATTERN box — the desired outcome of the loop — is filled red, the colour conventionally reserved for error or failure, while the ASSUMPTION box is blue and the DERIVED box green. The colour assignment encodes no stated meaning, and red simultaneously marks the pattern box and the feedback arrow, so it carries two unrelated meanings.
evidence: Rendered page: box 1 blue, box 2 green, box 3 red; the 'feedback' / 'adjust + pick pattern' arrow is also red.
acceptance_test: Re-map the palette so the pattern/outcome box is not red (or add a legend stating that red marks the selected patterns), and confirm the figure remains interpretable in grayscale — boxes are already distinguished by their numbered headers and by position, so no information should depend on hue.

issue: The caption describes the loop's mechanics but not what the reader should learn, and its parenthetical is ambiguously scoped: '(box 1) holds assumed scenario inputs, not instrumented FACTs' attaches to the end of the chain 'ASSUMPTION → DERIVED → PATTERN → ASSUMPTION', so it can be read as saying the whole loop holds assumptions rather than only the ASSUMPTION node.
evidence: Rendered page caption: 'FIGURE 26.2: Pattern Application Diagram: the Pattern-Measurement-Feedback Loop applied to the capstone scenario, closing the loop ASSUMPTION → DERIVED → PATTERN → ASSUMPTION (box 1) holds assumed scenario inputs, not instrumented FACTs.'
acceptance_test: Rewrite the caption to state the takeaway (e.g., 'the loop is closed by measurement: an assumption that fails validation returns to box 1 for adjustment, and only measured FACTs may enter the decision') and re-scope the parenthetical to the word ASSUMPTION it describes.

issue: The caption promises 'total vs activated parameters', but the chart encodes only the active fraction; the totals appear solely as small right-hand annotations. The comparison the caption advertises is therefore not visible in the plot, and the reader must read the annotation text to recover the totals.
evidence: Rendered page: x axis 'Active parameters as % of total', 0–10; totals (284B, 2800B, 125B, 320B) appear only in the small gray annotations at the right of each bar.
acceptance_test: Either add the counts to the y-axis tick labels (e.g., 'DeepSeek V4-Flash — 284B total / 13B active') so the caption's claim is visible in the plot, or narrow the caption to 'active fraction of total parameters'.

issue: The figure footnote is grammatically broken and, in a book that carefully distinguishes 'parameter' from 'parameters', reads as a typo: 'excluding the 51B in-gram embedding and 48 MTP VENDOR-REPORTED parameter; parameter varies across vendors.' The final clause's antecedent is also unclear.
evidence: Rendered page footnote as quoted; the sentence mixes a singular 'parameter' with a plural subject and ends with a clause whose referent is not stated.
acceptance_test: Rewrite as: '* Qwen bar = backbone ratio (125B backbone), excluding the 51B in-gram embedding and the 48 MTP vendor-reported parameters; denominators vary by vendor.' Confirm the footnote renders at ≥8 pt.

issue: The right-hand count annotations ('284B/13B active', '2800B/104B active', '125B backbone/6B active (+51B in-gram, 48 MTP)', '320B/18B active') and the footnote are set in small light-grey type — the lightest and smallest text in the figure — and the Qwen annotation is both the longest and the smallest, so the most caveat-heavy row is the least legible.
evidence: Rendered page at 150 dpi: annotation text is visibly smaller and lighter than the bold orange bar value labels ('4.6%', '3.7%', '4.8%', '5.6%').
acceptance_test: Measure rendered sizes and bring annotations and footnote to ≥8 pt with sufficient contrast (darker grey or black); confirm the Qwen annotation still fits without colliding with its bar value label.

issue: The in-figure title 'Extreme sparsity: single-digit active (2026)' and the caption's '2026 frontier MoE extreme sparsity' date the figure but do not scope it. The appendix elsewhere acknowledges a fifth 2026 family (Ornith-1.5-397B, released 2026-08-19) that is not plotted, so 'four open models' can read as an exhaustive survey of 2026 rather than four selected families.
evidence: Printed p. 421: 'Four 2026 frontier open models we surveyed converge on a second-order architectural pattern'. Printed p. 427: 'Beyond the four families above, Ornith-1.5-397B (released 2026-08-19 by DeepReinforce / orrist15-a1) ships as another natively multimodal frontier model'.
acceptance_test: Scope the title/caption explicitly (e.g., 'four selected 2026 open-weight MoE families; see A.6 for a fifth') and confirm the reader is not invited to read the four bars as an exhaustive 2026 survey.

figure: Table — Ch 26 workload matrix, 'First strategy to evaluate' column
issue: The last column is set far too narrow for its content, producing six-line wraps ('Precision-aware optimization (LoRA/QLoRA before full FT; gradient checkpointing (Ch 7))'), while the first three columns carry short entries with generous width. Row height is driven entirely by one column, and 'Real-time multimodal' wraps unnecessarily.
evidence: Rendered page: 'Workload' and 'Input' columns occupy roughly 40% of the table width for entries of one or two words; 'First strategy to evaluate' occupies roughly 25% and wraps to six lines in the Fine-tuning row.
acceptance_test: Rebalance the column widths (narrow Workload/Input, widen the strategy column) or move the strategy column to a second line spanning the row; confirm no cell wraps to more than three lines and the table still fits the text block.

issue: The 'Input' cell for the real-time multimodal row reads 'Med', an abbreviation used nowhere else in the table or in the visible prose, for a quantity whose unit (tokens? seconds? modality?) is never stated. The adjacent 'Output' cell ('Short (streamed)') is spelled out, so the two cells are not parallel in form.
evidence: Rendered page row: 'Real-time multimodal | Med | Short (streamed) | Latency + pipeline sync | Chunked prefill, streaming decode, P/D (Ch 8, 20)'.
acceptance_test: Spell the cell out and give the unit (e.g., 'Medium-length input (tokens)') or define 'Med' in the table's note; confirm the Input and Output cells use the same form in every row.

issue: The column headers 'KV cache*' and 'Compute*' assert a single comparable metric across all three rows, but the rows measure different quantities in different units. The DeepSeek rows report per-token quantities (bytes/token for KV; total FLOPs/token for compute); the GLM row reports per-layer quantities (bytes/layer for KV; attention FLOPs per head per layer for compute). A reader scanning the bold percentages (7%, 10%, 23%, 27%, 33%) will compare across rows — e.g. read 'GLM's 23% KV vs DeepSeek's 7%' as a model-to-model KV comparison — even though the scope is stated only in small italic sub-labels, a generic asterisk footnote, and the caption. The figure's own red callout forbids exactly the comparison its table layout invites.
evidence: Rendered page 448: headers 'KV cache*' / 'Compute*' in bold black; row sub-labels 'single-token KV cache', 'single-token inference FLOPs' (DeepSeek) vs 'BF16 / layer', 'attention only per head / layer' (GLM). Footnote reads only '*Metric scopes differ. 7% remaining = 93% reduction.' Caption states the scope difference in prose only. The two DeepSeek rows and the GLM row therefore share a column whose unit changes between rows (per-token vs per-layer; total vs attention-only).
acceptance_test: A reader who sees only the table (headers + cells, no caption) cannot state a false cross-row comparison. Concretely: either the headers themselves carry the scope ('KV cache — scope varies*', 'Compute metric — scope varies*'), or a 'scope' column states the unit per row, or the figure is split into two sub-tables (DeepSeek / GLM) with no shared numeric column.

issue: The DeepSeek rows omit the two parameters that determine per-token KV bytes — numeric precision and KV-head configuration (GQA group size) — while the GLM row does state precision ('BF16 / layer'). The 7% and 10% retentions are therefore not reproducible from the figure, and the reader cannot tell whether the vendor's ratio is precision-normalized (i.e. whether the reduction comes from fewer KV heads, lower precision, or both). The caption defers the 're-derivation caveat' to a paragraph below the figure, so the figure itself is not self-contained for its own headline numbers.
evidence: Rendered page 448: DeepSeek V4-Flash row reads '100% → ~7% (single-token KV cache)' and '100% → ~10% (single-token inference FLOPs)' with no precision or head-count qualifier; GLM-5.3-Flash row reads '100% → ~23% (BF16 / layer)'. Caption: 'See the paragraph below for the Fig 7.1 link and the re-derivation caveat.'
acceptance_test: For every row the figure states (a) numeric precision and (b) KV-head configuration, or explicitly states that the source does not report them (e.g. 'DeepSeek ratios as reported; precision and KV-head count not stated in source'). A reader can then say whether the 93% KV reduction is attributable to GQA, precision, or an unreported combination.

issue: Unexplained color coding of the model names: 'DeepSeek V4-Flash' is red, 'DeepSeek V4-Pro' is blue, 'GLM-5.3-Flash' is green, with no legend anywhere in the figure or caption. The two rows of the same family (DeepSeek V4) carry different hues, which implies a distinction the figure never defines and that contradicts the figure's own statement that the rows are 'one row per reported model'. In grayscale the three hues collapse to nearly the same mid-gray, so the coding carries no information in print.
evidence: Rendered page 448, first column: 'DeepSeek V4-Flash' in red, 'DeepSeek V4-Pro' in blue, 'GLM-5.3-Flash' in green. No key for these colors appears in the figure, the source line, or the caption.
acceptance_test: Either all model names are set in one color, or the colors encode a defined property (e.g. family) with a legend and a redundant non-color cue (grouping rule, indentation, or family sub-heading). DeepSeek V4-Flash and DeepSeek V4-Pro must not carry different hues unless the difference is defined.

issue: Label-scope mismatch between figure and caption. The in-figure source line labels the whole value set 'Value source: vendor-reported [1P]', but the caption splits the same values: '[1P] vendor-reported ratios; [DERIVED] the derived retentions shown in the figure.' The '100% → ~7%' style retentions are derived from reported reductions, so the figure's own label is broader than the caption's and a reader who reads only the figure will treat the derived retentions as first-party reported values.
evidence: Rendered page 448 source line: 'Value source: vendor-reported [1P] — DeepSeek V4: arXiv 2606.19348; GLM: z.ai/blog/glm-5.3-flash (2026-08-26). Vendor claims, not reproduced.' Caption: '[1P] vendor-reported ratios; [DERIVED] the derived retentions shown in the figure.'
acceptance_test: The figure's own source line distinguishes the two provenance classes, e.g. 'vendor-reported [1P] reductions; retentions [DERIVED]'. The figure and caption then assign the same label to the same span.

issue: The footnote demonstrates the 'remaining vs reduction' equivalence for one value only ('7% remaining = 93% reduction'), leaving the reader to infer whether the same holds for 10%, 23%, 27% and 33%. The rule is stated once but illustrated once, and the illustrated case is the one most likely to be misread (a 7% figure looks like a typo).
evidence: Rendered page 448 footnote: '*Metric scopes differ. 7% remaining = 93% reduction.'
acceptance_test: The footnote states the rule once for all rows (e.g. 'x% remaining = (100 − x)% reduction; scopes differ — see row labels') or the equivalence is shown for every row.

issue: Alignment mismatch: all four column headers are centred while every data cell is left-aligned, so the header-to-cell association is weaker than it needs to be for a table whose whole purpose is a four-column comparison. There are no column rules either, so the reader must rely on whitespace alone.
evidence: Rendered page 448: headers 'reported model | own baseline | KV cache* | Compute*' centred over the column band; row content ('vs V3.2', '100% → ~7%', '100% → ~10%') left-aligned beneath them.
acceptance_test: Each header is aligned with the content of its own column (left-align headers over left-aligned cells, or right-align numeric columns and their headers), and the scan path from header to value is unambiguous at print size.

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The SYSTEM / MODEL grouping is marked only by an unlabeled horizontal rule and two small rotated labels set beside a single red vertical arrow. The rule stops short of the arrow (it spans the band width only), so the arrow appears to run continuously across the boundary; nothing in the drawing states whether the arrow is one continuum spanning both groups or two separate scope brackets. The rotated labels' vertical extent is also undetermined — 'SYSTEM' sits at the midpoint of the blue group and 'MODEL' at the midpoint of the green group, but neither is bounded. The figure's central claim (system-side vs model-side placement) therefore rests on a boundary the reader must infer from colour alone.
evidence: Rendered page 452: red vertical arrow at the far left with a single arrowhead at the top of the stack; rotated 'SYSTEM' label beside the five blue bands; rotated 'MODEL' label beside the three green bands; a black horizontal rule between 'Inside post-training' and 'Inside MoE routing' that does not touch the arrow.
acceptance_test: The SYSTEM/MODEL boundary is explicit in the drawing: either two separate arrows (one spanning the blue bands, one spanning the green bands, each with its own arrowhead and label), or labelled group brackets, or a boundary rule that reaches and is labelled on the arrow. A reader can state, without the caption, which bands are system-side and which are model-side.

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The upward red arrowhead is the figure's only directional element and is the most likely source of the 'higher = better / more advanced' reading that the caption explicitly disclaims ('not a ranking of superiority: a lower band is not "better" or "worse" than a higher one'). The caption never explains what the arrow means; its meaning appears only in the small red sub-caption ('scope of placement: intelligence shifts up out of the weights'). The figure therefore asserts a directional trend in its drawing while its caption denies a ranking, and the reader must reconcile two different messages from two different typographic registers.
evidence: Rendered page 452: red arrow with a single upward arrowhead spanning the stack; sub-caption in small red type 'scope of placement: intelligence shifts up out of the weights'; caption 'The horizontal bands are a design choice (which layer owns which capability), not a ranking of superiority…'. The caption contains no reference to the arrow.
acceptance_test: The caption states what the arrow encodes (e.g. 'the arrow marks the historical direction of capability migration, not a ranking'), and the arrow is either labelled in-figure or drawn so it cannot be read as a preference ordering (e.g. double-headed or non-directional connector).

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The legend gloss 'blue = where the system runs · green = where the model runs' is inaccurate for the 'Inside post-training' band, which is a development-time activity rather than a runtime location, and the within-hue lightness ramp (dark at the top of each group, light at the bottom) is never explained even though it encodes vertical position. The reader is left to guess what shade depth means.
evidence: Rendered page 452: bands 'Across a fleet of models' (darkest navy) → 'Inside post-training' (lightest blue); 'Inside MoE routing' (darkest green) → 'Inside weights' (lightest green). Legend line: 'blue = where the system runs · green = where the model runs'. No key for shade depth.
acceptance_test: The legend states both encodings: hue = system-side vs model-side placement, and shade depth = vertical position (further from the weights = darker). The gloss is reworded so it is true of every band (e.g. 'blue = system-side placement · green = model-side placement').

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The caption's evidence label is truncated: it terminates on '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' with no noun, whereas the parallel caption on the facing figure (A.3) reads '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual band structure; [DERIVED] era markers'. As printed, the label is not a complete label and cannot be matched against the book's evidence-label vocabulary.
evidence: Rendered page 452 caption ends: '…not "what is best here." [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual'. Rendered page 451 caption ends: '…[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual band structure; [DERIVED] era markers'.
acceptance_test: The caption's label is a complete, defined label from the book's vocabulary (e.g. '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual placement map'), matching the form used in Figure A.3.

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The subtitle's parenthetical '(Appendix A. "Where Should Intelligence Live?")' uses a full stop after 'Appendix A' and gives no section number, while the neighbouring figure's sub-caption cites a numbered subsection ('Appendix A.8'). The two appendix cross-references are therefore not in the same form, and the reader is sent to a section title rather than a locatable section.
evidence: Rendered page 452 subtitle: '(Appendix A. "Where Should Intelligence Live?")'. Rendered page 451 sub-caption: 'the spine of this handbook (Appendix A.8).'
acceptance_test: Both appendix cross-references use the same numbered form (e.g. 'Appendix A.8' / 'Appendix A.9'), and each resolves to the section that actually contains the referenced material.

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The eight chapter cross-references are unverified and internally suspicious: 'Ch.8' is cited for three bands with three different subjects — 'Inside test-time search' (Ch.8, Ch.20), 'Inside attention' (Ch.7, Ch.8) and 'Inside weights' (Ch.3, Ch.8). A single chapter can legitimately span several of these, but the figure gives no indication of what Ch.8 covers, so the reader cannot tell whether the citation is a deliberate umbrella reference or a copy error. The same applies to 'Ch.24', cited for both 'Inside agent runtime' and 'Inside tools'.
evidence: Rendered page 452 right-hand column: 'Ch.18, Ch.20' / 'Ch.17–20, Ch.24' / 'Ch.19, Ch.24' / 'Ch.8, Ch.20' / 'Ch.19, Ch.21' / 'Ch.10' / 'Ch.7, Ch.8' / 'Ch.3, Ch.8'.
acceptance_test: Each of the eight references resolves to a chapter whose subject matches the band label, and any chapter cited for three or more bands is one whose scope genuinely covers all three (otherwise the citation is corrected or the band is re-pointed). Verified against the table of contents.

figure: FIGURE A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: 'Inside post-training' is a development-time activity, not a runtime placement location, so it does not sit on the same axis as the other seven bands ('Inside weights', 'Inside attention', 'Inside MoE routing', 'Inside test-time search', 'Inside tools', 'Inside agent runtime', 'Across a fleet of models'), all of which describe where capability sits while a system is running. The figure's own axis label is 'WHERE it lives', which post-training does not satisfy — post-training produces weights rather than hosting capability at inference time.
evidence: Rendered page 452: band 'Inside post-training — Ch.19, Ch.21' sits in the blue group with the axis label 'vertical axis = WHERE it lives: nonexclusive placement choices, not a ranking'.
acceptance_test: Either the post-training band is visually marked as a build-time band (distinct hatch or a 'build-time' tag) so it is not read as a runtime placement, or the axis label is broadened to cover it (e.g. 'where capability is invested') and the caption notes that post-training is upstream of the weights band.

figure: FIGURE A.3 — A conceptual layering of frontier AI systems
issue: The bands are drawn as a contiguous, gapless stack, which is the standard visual grammar for a substrate/dependency hierarchy — each layer resting on the one below. The caption disclaims precisely that reading ('the vertical stacking is a layering … not a causal lineage: a later layer does not require the one below it'), but the disclaimer is textual only and the drawing carries the stronger, wrong signal. A reader who skims the figure will retain the dependency reading.
evidence: Rendered page 451: nine bands stacked with no vertical gaps and no separating rules; caption: 'the vertical stacking is a layering (which capabilities sit on which substrate), not a causal lineage: a later layer does not require the one below it, and the eras overlap.'
acceptance_test: The drawing itself carries the non-dependency reading: visible gaps between bands, a left-hand bracket labelled 'capability stack — not a dependency chain', or a legend entry stating 'stacked for display; no layer requires the one below'. A reader who sees only the drawing does not infer a dependency chain.

figure: FIGURE A.3 — A conceptual layering of frontier AI systems
issue: Legend typography is inconsistent with the rest of the book: the third legend entry begins with a lowercase word ('fleet (thick)') where the other two are capitalised ('Model architecture', 'Capability-led'), and it uses straight double quotes around 'intelligence placement' while the figure's own caption uses typographic quotes ('what caused what'). The legend also mixes capitalization inside a single entry ('foundation, efficiency, MoE').
evidence: Rendered page 451 legend: 'Model architecture (dashed) — foundation, efficiency, MoE; darker shade = MoE' / 'Capability-led (solid) — reasoning / test-time / agentic' / 'fleet (thick) — multi-model "intelligence placement"'. Caption on the same page uses curly quotes.
acceptance_test: All three legend entries begin with a capitalised term and use the book's typographic quotation marks; capitalization within entries is consistent.

figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: In the 'Actual stop' row, a solid flow arrow enters the dashed 'pass 3' box and a second solid arrow leaves it toward 'exit'. The figure's own legend defines 'Solid arrows = flow', so the drawing asserts a flow into a node the figure simultaneously declares 'not executed'. The reader can legitimately infer that pass 3 runs and is then discarded — which is precisely the outcome the caption denies ('A true exit omits later work'). The figure's central distinction is undercut by its own arrow convention.
evidence: Rendered page 459, 'Actual stop' row: pass 1 → pass 2 → [dashed 'pass 3' box, 'not executed' beneath] → [orange 'exit' box]; both connectors appear solid. Legend: 'Dashed arrows = weight reuse; dashed box = not executed' and 'Solid arrows = flow; labeled boxes mark exit / selection'.
acceptance_test: No solid 'flow' arrow enters or leaves the not-executed box. Either the exit arrow runs directly from pass 2 and the dashed 'pass 3 (not executed)' box is placed off the flow path with no connectors, or the connectors into/out of it are dashed and the legend states that dashed connectors also mean 'skipped'. A reader tracing only the arrows cannot conclude that pass 3 executed.

figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: The 'not executed' annotation is set outside the dashed box, in the smallest type on the page, and is the only element preventing the misreading identified in FIG-A5-01. Its placement and size make it the first thing to be lost at print size or in a grayscale reproduction.
evidence: Rendered page 459: 'not executed' appears in small type centred beneath the dashed 'pass 3' box, outside its border, smaller than the box labels 'pass 1' / 'pass 2' / 'pass 3'.
acceptance_test: 'not executed' is set inside the dashed box as a second line at the same size as the other box labels, or the box label itself reads 'pass 3 (not executed)'.

figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: The legend line 'Shared core weights and iteration caches are unchanged above; omitted here for clarity' is ambiguous: 'unchanged above' can be read as 'the weights are frozen / unchanged (as in training)' rather than 'the same as in the upper diagram'. The intended meaning — that the shared weight set and the per-iteration caches drawn in the upper half are simply not repeated in the two lower paths — is not the first reading.
evidence: Rendered page 459 legend, first line: 'Shared core weights and iteration caches are unchanged above; omitted here for clarity.'
acceptance_test: The line is reworded unambiguously, e.g. 'The shared weight set and the per-iteration caches shown in the upper diagram are omitted from the two paths below for clarity.'

figure: Figures A.2, A.3, A.4, A.5 (visual semantics)
issue: Red carries three unrelated meanings across the four appendix figures: a warning/callout in A.2 ('NOT A CROSS-MODEL PERFORMANCE RANKING'), an axis/annotation device in A.4 (the vertical arrow, the 'Model intelligence ≠ system intelligence' box, the red sub-caption), and a data category in A.5 (the red-outlined 'iteration N history cache' boxes). A reader who carries the A.2/A.4 reading of red into A.5 will read the iteration caches as a warning rather than as a state category.
evidence: Rendered pages 448 (red callout box and red model names), 452 (red arrow, red sub-caption, red-outlined box), 459 (red-outlined 'iteration 1/2/3 history cache' boxes).
acceptance_test: Red is reserved for one role across the appendix (annotations/callouts), and the iteration-cache boxes in A.5 use a distinct, consistent category colour that is also distinguishable in grayscale; or the legend in A.5 states that red-outlined boxes denote per-iteration state.

issue: All four figure pages are top-aligned with roughly the bottom quarter to third of the page left blank (the figure block ends around 60–75% of the text height on each page), and on pages 451 and 452 there is an additional loose gap between the italic sub-caption and the 'FIGURE A.x' caption. The result is four pages that read as under-filled and visually unbalanced for a book of this standard.
evidence: Rendered pages 448, 451, 452, 459: content ends at approximately y=600/760 (p.448), y=600/760 (p.451), y=610/760 (p.452), y=580/760 (p.459) in a 612×792 render, with the remainder blank.
acceptance_test: Each figure page is either vertically balanced (figure + caption block optically centred in the text block) or the trailing space is eliminated by pulling the following section onto the page. The gap between the sub-caption and the figure caption is tightened to the house figure-caption spacing.

issue: The smallest annotations in all four figures — Figure A.2's italic scope sub-labels ('single-token KV cache', 'single-token inference FLOPs', 'BF16 / layer') and its two-line source line; Figure A.3's legend text and '≈YYYY' era markers; Figure A.4's 'Ch.x' references and the red sub-caption; Figure A.5's four-line legend and 'not executed' — are set in small italic grey and are the elements most likely to fall below the 8 pt print floor or to lose contrast in a grayscale proof. At 150 dpi they are legible, but legibility at 150 dpi is not the acceptance criterion.
evidence: Rendered pages 448, 451, 452, 459: the annotations listed above are visibly smaller and lighter than all other figure text; the Figure A.5 legend is four lines of small italic set below the diagram.
acceptance_test: A 100% print proof of each figure page confirms every in-figure annotation is at or above 8 pt and holds contrast in grayscale; any annotation that fails is enlarged, re-set in roman, or moved into the caption.

figure: Figure 7.5 (KV cache size vs context, by attention geometry)
issue: The caption's stated formula for KV bytes per token omits the factor of 2 for the K and V tensors, so the formula as printed does not reproduce the figure's own numbers.
evidence: Caption: 'KV per token is set by the attention shape (layers x KV heads x head_dim x precision) x bytes'. Substituting the caption's own canonical geometry (80 layers x 64 KV heads x 128 head_dim x 2 B) = 1,310,720 B = 1.31 MB/token. That is the 8-bit number, not the 2.62 MB/token the caption and the figure legend use for FP16. The missing factor is 2 (K and V). A reader who follows the printed formula gets exactly half the value and will conclude the figure's FP16 curve is wrong.
acceptance_test: Caption formula must read '2 (K and V) x layers x KV heads x head_dim x bytes/element' and must reproduce 2.62 MB/token (FP16) and 1.31 MB/token (8-bit) for the canonical 80-layer geometry, with the substitution shown or checkable.

issue: The caption states a '64:1 query-to-KV head ratio' and simultaneously claims the KV footprint is '8x smaller'. These are mutually inconsistent, and the 64:1 figure also contradicts Figure 7.1.
evidence: Caption: 'GQA with a 64:1 query-to-KV head ratio is 8x smaller.' A 64:1 ratio implies 64x, not 8x. The figure's own legend gives GQA FP16 ~0.33 MB/tok = 2.62/8, i.e. 8x. Figure 7.1 (PDF 131 / printed 111) labels the same geometry '8 query heads : 1 KV head (x 8 groups)' = 64 query heads over 8 KV heads = 8:1. The caption is the only place the 64:1 appears, and it is wrong.
acceptance_test: Caption must read '8:1 (64 query heads sharing 8 KV heads)' or the reduction must be restated as 64x with the legend values changed. Figure 7.1's label, Figure 7.5's legend, and Figure 7.5's caption must agree on one ratio.

issue: The scale segments are not drawn to scale: the NVFP4 '2 B scales' segment is drawn with the same width as the MXFP4 '1 B scale' segment, which contradicts the figure's own subtitle and destroys the figure's entire point (that NVFP4's scale bill is twice MXFP4's).
evidence: Subtitle: 'Payload and local-scale bar widths are proportional to bytes.' In the 150-dpi render, the value segments are drawn at roughly 21 px/B (row 1: 16 B over ~340 px; row 2: two 8 B segments over ~340 px), but the dark scale segment occupies the same horizontal extent in both rows (~23 px), i.e. 1 B in both. The two bars also span the same total width although they represent 17 B and 18 B. The caption's hedge ('Bars are proportional only for local scales and local-scale bytes') does not license this and is itself incoherent.
acceptance_test: Render at 300 dpi and measure: dark-segment widths must satisfy w_NVFP4 / w_MXFP4 = 2.0 +/- 0.1, and total bar widths must satisfy W_NVFP4 / W_MXFP4 = 18/17 = 1.059 +/- 0.01. If not-to-scale drawing is intended, delete the subtitle clause 'Payload and local-scale bar widths are proportional to bytes' and add 'scale segments drawn not to scale' to the caption.

issue: The full-fine-tune bar (~1120 GB) cannot be reconstructed from the components the figure's own note lists, and the note explicitly excludes the only term that could explain the gap.
evidence: Note: 'Full fine-tune: FP16 weights + FP16 grads + Adam m/v (2xFP32) + activation memory' followed by 'Activation, microbatch/sequence, and offload/checkpointing are NOT included'. Recomputation: 70e9 x 2 B = 140 GB (FP16 weights) + 70e9 x 2 B = 140 GB (FP16 grads) + 2 x 70e9 x 4 B = 560 GB (Adam m and v in FP32) = 840 GB. The bar is labelled ~1120 GB, a 280 GB residual. 280 GB is exactly one FP32 copy of the parameters (FP32 master weights), which the note does not list. The note's own framing ('Each bar is a conditional floor (weights + the listed states...)') requires the bar to equal the listed states; it does not.
acceptance_test: Either (a) the note lists FP32 master weights (280 GB) and the bar remains ~1120 GB, or (b) the bar becomes ~840 GB and the caption's '~1,120 GB' is updated. A reader must be able to reconstruct every bar from the note's component list with zero residual.

issue: The QLoRA bar (~60 GB) is not reconstructible from the components the note lists, and the bar's own axis label ('weights+adapters') contradicts the arithmetic that would produce 60 GB.
evidence: Note: 'QLoRA: 4-bit (NF4) base + LoRA adapters + a small optimizer.' Recomputation: 70e9 x 0.5 B = 35 GB for the 4-bit base; adapters and optimizer are stated as small, giving ~35-40 GB, not 60 GB. The value 60 GB is reproduced almost exactly by 35 GB (4-bit base) + 24.1 GB (canonical 9.2K FP16 KV, the same 24.1 GB used in the inference bar: 140 + 24.1 = 164.1 ~ 165 GB) = 59.1 GB. So the bar appears to include KV, which the note omits and the bar label excludes. The caption's range '~50-70 GB' is consistent with the bar but not with the note.
acceptance_test: State the composition on the figure (e.g. '4-bit base 35 GB + KV 24 GB + adapters/optimizer ~1 GB') and relabel the bar 'weights + KV + adapters'; or reduce the bar to ~36-40 GB and narrow the caption's range to match. The caption range must bracket the bar's stated composition.

figure: Figure 6.2 (Latency distribution: the mean hides the tail)
issue: The caption attributes the exceedance to a TTFT threshold, but the plotted quantity is request latency; the caveat that this is a superset of TTFT violations lives only in the prose on the previous page, not on the figure or in its caption.
evidence: Figure x-axis: 'Request latency (s)'; shaded band: 'SLO-violating region (> 2 s)'; vertical line: 'SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)'. Caption: '1% of requests exceed the 2 s TTFT threshold'. The prose on PDF 114 / printed 94 states the correct relationship ('Request latency != TTFT, so a TTFT-budget line drawn on request latency flags a superset of TTFT violations'), but the figure sits on the next page and the caption does not carry the caveat. A reader who sees only the figure will read the band as a TTFT violation rate.
acceptance_test: Caption must state that the plotted quantity is request latency and that the 2 s TTFT budget drawn on it flags a superset of TTFT violations; the band label should read '> 2 s (TTFT budget drawn on request latency)'.

issue: The '9.5K' annotation is unexplained in the caption and uses a different canonical context length than Figure 7.6 for the same scenario.
evidence: The annotation '9.5K x 24.9 GB (FP16 bound)' is internally consistent (9,500 x 2.62 MB = 24.9 GB) but the caption never mentions 9.5K or 24.9 GB, and the notation '9.5K x 24.9 GB' reads as a product rather than '9.5K tokens -> 24.9 GB'. Figure 7.6 (PDF 147 / printed 127) states the canonical input as 'max 9.2K canonical input' and derives 24.1 GB of KV there (140 + 24.1 = 164.1 ~ 165 GB). The two figures therefore use different canonical context lengths (9.5K vs 9.2K) for the same canonical scenario, and the house convention fixes 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200.
acceptance_test: One canonical context length must be used in both figures (9.2K), and the annotation must name what it is (e.g. 'canonical 9.2K-token context -> 24.1 GB FP16 KV'); the caption must reference the annotation explicitly.

issue: A dangling annotation states a per-token rate that the legend already gives for the entire line, at a specific x-position, with no stated consequence and no caption coverage.
evidence: The label '12.6K = 0.33 MB/tok' sits beside the GQA FP16 marker at x ~ 12.6K. The per-token rate 0.33 MB/tok is already in the legend and applies to the whole line, so the annotation conveys nothing on its own. The implied derived quantity is 12.6K x 0.33 MB ~ 4.2 GB, which is never shown. The caption does not mention it.
acceptance_test: Either remove the annotation or restate it as a derived quantity ('12.6K tokens -> 4.2 GB GQA FP16 KV') and add one caption sentence explaining the point being made.

figure: Figure 7.5 (annotations '8x scaling: full-MHA FP16' and '8x scaling: GQA FP16')
issue: Two annotations both labelled '8x scaling' attached to two different curves are self-contradictory on a literal reading and duplicate an unambiguous marker already present.
evidence: The chart carries a clear '8x' label with a vertical double arrow between the red and blue curves near x = 10, which already communicates the ratio. The two longer labels, '8x scaling: full-MHA FP16' (near the red curve at x ~ 100-200) and '8x scaling: GQA FP16' (near the blue curve at x ~ 100), read as if both curves are '8x scaled', which would make their ratio 1 rather than 8. A reader can also misread '8x scaling' as 'scales 8x with context', which is false for every curve (all are linear in context).
acceptance_test: Replace the two labels with a single annotation on the existing vertical arrow, e.g. 'full-MHA FP16 = 8 x GQA FP16 at the same context', and delete the ambiguous pair.

issue: The legend labels the 8-bit full-MHA series as 'FP16', while the parallel 8-bit GQA series is correctly labelled 'FP8'.
evidence: Legend entries: 'full-MHA FP16 (bound, ~2.62 MB/tok)', 'full-MHA FP16 (raw byte-halving, 50%)', 'GQA FP16 (~0.33 MB/tok)', 'GQA FP8 (raw, ~0.16 MB/tok)'. The caption confirms the orange series is the 8-bit curve ('FP16 = 2.62 MB/token, FP8:8-bit = 1.31'). A reader scanning the legend sees two 'full-MHA FP16' series and cannot tell which is 8-bit without reading the caption.
acceptance_test: Rename the entry to 'full-MHA 8-bit (raw byte-halving of FP16, ~1.31 MB/tok)'; no legend entry may label an 8-bit series as FP16.

issue: The label '(x 8 groups)' is ambiguous against a drawing that shows three groups plus an ellipsis, and it sits inside the box the caption calls the load-bearing number.
evidence: The figure draws three groups of eight query-head glyphs, each feeding one K/V box, followed by an ellipsis at both the query-head and K/V levels. The label box reads '8 query heads : 1 KV head (x 8 groups)'. '(x 8 groups)' can be read as 'eight groups are drawn' (false) or 'the pattern repeats eight times' (true). The caption explicitly says the load-bearing number is the n_q:n_kv ratio, so the parenthetical must not be the ambiguous part.
acceptance_test: Label reads '8 query heads : 1 KV head per group (8 groups total; 3 shown)'.

figure: Figure 6.2 annotation box vs Section 6.3.1 prose
issue: The figure reports a sample mean of 0.85 s while the prose calls the mean of that same stream 0.84 s; the two quantities are different and the prose conflates them.
evidence: Prose: 'The mean of that stream is ~ 0.99 x 0.8 + 0.01 x 5.0 = 0.84 s'. Figure annotation box: 'mean = 0.85s'. The 0.84 s expression is the two-point approximation; the plotted sample's mean is 0.85 s because the log-normal body is right-skewed and its mean exceeds its median. The prose's phrase 'the mean of that stream' attaches the approximation to the sample.
acceptance_test: Prose must distinguish the two-point approximation (~0.84 s) from the plotted sample mean (0.85 s), or the figure's box must print 0.84 s; the two must not both claim to be 'the mean of that stream'.

issue: Two of the four data series are distinguished only by colour, so the chart degrades in grayscale and for colour-vision-deficient readers.
evidence: Series markers: full-MHA FP16 = red circle, full-MHA 8-bit = orange square, GQA FP16 = blue upward triangle, GQA FP8 = green upward triangle. The two GQA series share a marker shape and differ only in hue; at the small marker size used, blue and green have similar relative luminance. The two horizontal reference lines (black dashed 640 GB, blue dashed 436 GB) also compete with the blue data series.
acceptance_test: Give GQA FP8 a distinct marker shape (e.g. inverted triangle or diamond) and confirm all four series remain distinguishable when the page is rendered in grayscale.

issue: The fine-tune (red) and QLoRA (green) bars have nearly identical grayscale luminance, and the blue reference line shares the inference bar's hue.
evidence: Bars: inference = blue, full fine-tune = red, QLoRA = green. Red and green map to nearly the same relative luminance in grayscale, so the two bars are distinguished only by height and by their direct value labels. The '8xH100 (640 GB)' legend line is blue, the same hue as the inference bar.
acceptance_test: Differentiate the three bars by fill pattern or luminance step (solid / hatched / light) and verify the page remains readable in grayscale.

issue: The p90 and p95 reference lines share both colour and dash pattern and are separated by only 0.05 s, so they are effectively indistinguishable in grayscale.
evidence: Vertical percentile markers: p50 0.80 (green dashed), p90 0.94 (red dashed), p95 0.99 (red dashed), p99 1.33 (blue dash-dot), SLO 2 s (blue dash-dot). The p90 and p95 lines are 0.05 s apart on a 0-6 s axis, i.e. under 1% of the plot width apart, and are rendered in the same colour and style.
acceptance_test: Give each percentile line a distinct dash pattern or a distinct marker, and verify in grayscale that p90 and p95 are separable.

figure: Figure 7.3 (Quantization choices are not execution guarantees)
issue: The fan-out from 'Runtime tensors in the kernel-required layout' to three boxes can be read as three sequential stages rather than three mutually exclusive execution paths.
evidence: The arrow labelled 'compatible dispatch' splits into 'Native FP4 math', 'Fused dequant', and 'Reconstruct'. The caption calls these 'execution paths' (plural, exclusive), but the drawing shows a single arrow reaching all three boxes with no exclusivity marker. The note 'Only supported combinations can load and execute' partly covers it but does not say that exactly one path is taken.
acceptance_test: Mark the fan-out as exclusive (a brace labelled 'exactly one supported path', or a 'one of' label on the arrow) so the drawing matches the caption's 'execution paths' wording.

issue: The caption's 'successive, not jointly retained' disclaimer is attached to the recurrent row but the figure's own note applies 'snapshots are schematic' to both rows, inviting the reader to misapply it to the KV row; the figure also does not name the model the caption cites.
evidence: Caption: 'Three token snapshots are schematic; recurrent snapshots are successive, not jointly retained.' Figure note: 'Arrows = token input / state flow; snapshots are schematic.' The bottom row is cumulative (the third snapshot shows KV1 KV2 KV3), so a reader who generalises the disclaimer to that row will conclude the wrong thing about KV retention. The caption cites 'Configuration-backed example (Qwen3.8-27B)' but the figure subtitle does not.
acceptance_test: Caption must state that the KV row is cumulative (snapshot 3 retains KV1-KV3) while the recurrent row shows only the current state; add the model name to the figure subtitle.

issue: The caption's proportionality sentence is incoherent, and its exclusion list omits the NVFP4 per-tensor FP32 global scale that the figure itself flags as outside the 18 B local total.
evidence: Caption: 'Bars are proportional only for local scales and local-scale bytes.' This is not a well-formed statement: the bars are either proportional to bytes or they are not. The figure states 'NVFP4 global FP32 scale: 4 B per tensor, not per block', but the caption's exclusion list ('padding, headers, extra copies and high-precision exceptions') does not include it, so a reader may add the 4 B to the 18 B total or may not, with no guidance. Including it would give 22 B / 32 = 0.6875 B/value = 5.5 bit/value.
acceptance_test: Caption states the proportionality rule in one unambiguous sentence and lists the per-tensor FP32 scale among the excluded items (or adds it to the total with the resulting bit/value shown).

issue: The chart draws the 436 GB KV budget but never marks the context length at which each curve crosses it, which is the single most decision-relevant number the chart can supply.
evidence: For full-MHA FP16 the crossing is 436 GB / 2.62 MB/token ~ 166K tokens; for GQA FP16 it is ~1.33M tokens (off the plotted axis). page: PDF 181 / printed 161 (equation); FIG 9.1 on PDF 177 / printed 157; prose on PDF 176 / printed 156
figure: FIG 9.1 (model) vs. the ring-latency equation in §9.3
issue: The ring-latency equation in §9.3 omits the factor of 2 for the two phases of an all-reduce, so its own printed substitution does not produce the printed result, and the equation contradicts the model drawn in FIG 9.1 and the prose on printed p.156.
evidence: Printed on p.161: 'T_ring ≈ (N−1)/N · M/R_eff ≈ 7/8 · 140 GB / 40 GB/s ≈ 6.1 s'. Substitution: 7/8 = 0.875; 140/40 = 3.5; 0.875 × 3.5 = 3.06 s — a factor of 2 short of the printed 6.1 s. The correct ring all-reduce critical path is 2(N−1)/N · M/R_eff = 1.75 × 140/40 = 6.125 s, which is exactly the model drawn in FIG 9.1 ('sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes', '140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75×)', 'HDR 6,125 ms') and the prose on printed p.156 ('the eight-rank ring on 8×3 instead sends 245 GB per rank: about 0.54 s at the H100 directional peak, 6.1 s at an assumed effective ... 40 GB/s'). FIG 9.2 independently confirms the 2(N−1)/N form: 12 B sent for a 4-element FP16 input = 1.5× = 2(N−1)/N at N=4. The finding holds even if a '2' is present in the source formula, because the printed substitution '7/8 · 140 GB / 40 GB/s' omits it.
acceptance_test: In the source, change the equation to 'T_ring ≈ 2(N−1)/N · M/R_eff ≈ 2 × 7/8 × 140 GB / 40 GB/s ≈ 6.1 s' (equivalently '1.75 × 140 GB / 40 GB/s'), and add a clause naming the two phases ('reduce-scatter + all-gather'). Confirm that the printed 6.1 s, FIG 9.1's 245 GB / 6,125 ms, FIG 9.1's caption '6.1 s', and printed p.156's '6.1 s' all agree, then re-run the numeric regression gate over Chapter 9.

page: PDF 177 / printed 157 (legend and caption); also PDF 176 / printed 156 and PDF 181 / printed 161

issue: The legend label 'Two-way HDR' is ambiguous in a way that changes the answer by 2×, and the same 40 GB/s assumption is given three different names in the book (legend 'Two-way', p.156 'two-rank', p.161 '2 HDR rails/ports per node').
evidence: 'Two-way' most naturally reads as a bidirectional aggregate (send + receive on one link). Under that reading the ring moves 245 GB sent per rank at 20 GB/s per direction = 12.25 s, not the 6.1 s printed in the figure subtitle, the caption, and printed p.156. The book's own framing elsewhere is explicitly per-direction: printed p.161 states '490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time', i.e. 245 GB sent at 450 GB/s directional, and FIG 9.1's NVLink entry is labelled 'directional peak 450 GB/s'. The HDR entry is the only one whose directionality is unspecified, and it is the one whose label admits a 2× misreading.
acceptance_test: Choose one unambiguous descriptor for the 40 GB/s assumption and use it identically in the FIG 9.1 legend, the FIG 9.1 caption, printed p.156, and printed p.161. Recommended: 'HDR, 2 rails/node, assumed effective 40 GB/s per direction'. The words 'per direction' must appear in the legend entry so that the 245 GB / 40 GB/s = 6.125 s arithmetic is forced by the label rather than inferred.

issue: The subtitle says '140 GB tensor' while the x-axis says 'Logical input tensor per rank [GB]'; the per-rank qualifier is dropped exactly where the reader needs it to interpret the 1.75× factor.
evidence: Subtitle: 'N = 8; sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes / 140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75×)'. X-axis: 'Logical input tensor per rank [GB]'. Caption: 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size'. A reader who takes '140 GB tensor' as the whole collective payload would expect 1.75 × 140/8 GB per rank, not 245 GB.
acceptance_test: Change the subtitle to '140 GB per rank (245 GB sent at 1.75×)' so that the subtitle, the x-axis, and the caption use one qualifier.

issue: The figure asserts the 1.75× traffic factor without showing where it comes from, so the reader must take it on faith or reconstruct it from the caption.
evidence: Subtitle: 'sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes'. The factor is 2(N−1)/N = 2×7/8 = 1.75 for N=8 (reduce-scatter plus all-gather, each moving (N−1)/N of the tensor). Neither the figure nor the caption states this; the caption only says 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount.' The same unexplained constant appears in FIG 9.2 as '12 B sent' for an 8 B input (1.5× at N=4).
acceptance_test: Add the derivation to the subtitle, e.g. 'sent bytes per rank = 2(N−1)/N × tensor = 1.75 × tensor bytes', and mirror the same form in FIG 9.2's summary box ('12 B sent = 1.5 × 8 B input').

figure: FIG 9.2 subtitle: 'Four ranks; four FP16 elements per input (6 B/rank).'
issue: The parenthetical states the input size as 6 B/rank, but four FP16 elements are 8 B/rank; 6 B is the per-phase sent volume, not the input size. As written the figure's own headline number is wrong.
evidence: Four FP16 elements × 2 B = 8 B per rank of input. The figure body correctly shows '6 B sent + 6 B received/rank' per phase and 'Per rank: 12 B sent + 12 B received = 24 B endpoint total', and the caption says 'each rank sends 12 B and receives 12 B across both phases'. 12 B sent / 8 B input = 1.5 = 2(N−1)/N at N=4, which is the same factor FIG 9.1 uses at N=8 (1.75). If the input really were 6 B, the ratio would be 2.0, contradicting both figures. The parenthetical is attached to 'per input', so the natural reading is input size.
acceptance_test: Rewrite the subtitle as 'Four ranks; four FP16 elements per input (8 B/rank); 6 B sent + 6 B received per rank per phase' and confirm that 8 B input → 12 B sent → 1.5× is stated or derivable on the page. Re-check that no other caption or prose in Chapter 9 repeats the '6 B/rank' input figure.

figure: FIG 9.2 phase annotations ('3 neighbor rounds / 6 B sent + 6 B received/rank')
issue: '3 neighbor rounds' can be misread as '3 neighbors', but a four-rank ring has exactly two distinct neighbors per rank; the quantity being counted is rounds (steps), not neighbors.
evidence: The figure's own ring sub-diagram shows R0→R1→R2→R3→R0, i.e. two neighbors per rank. The correct count is 3 rounds (N−1 steps) per phase, each moving one 2 B chunk, as the separate note 'Each rank sends one 2 B chunk to the next rank' states.
acceptance_test: Change both phase annotations to '3 rounds (one 2 B chunk per round)' or '3 steps × 2 B = 6 B sent per rank', so that rounds and neighbors are not conflated.

figure: FIG 9.2 reduce-scatter row (Rank 0 → [10], Rank 1 → [20], Rank 2 → [-10], Rank 3 → [0])
issue: The figure asserts a specific chunk→rank ownership (rank r ends with reduced chunk r) without stating the chunk-flow convention, and the most commonly taught forward-flow convention yields rank r → chunk r+1. An expert reader who knows that convention will read the figure as wrong rather than as a convention choice.
evidence: With the textbook convention 'at step 0 rank r forwards its own chunk r to its successor', chunk j starts at rank j and completes at rank j−1, so rank r would hold chunk r+1 (rank 0 → 20, rank 1 → −10, rank 2 → 0, rank 3 → 10). The figure's assignment is nevertheless achievable — it corresponds to the variant where rank r forwards chunk r−1 first, so chunk j starts at rank j+1 and completes at rank j — but the figure shows only the neighbour order, not the chunk flow, so the reader cannot tell which convention is in force.
acceptance_test: Add one clause to the caption or the figure, e.g. 'chunk j is first forwarded by rank j+1, so rank r ends the reduce-scatter holding reduced chunk r', or annotate the ring sub-diagram with the chunk index in flight. Confirm that the stated convention reproduces the four reduce-scatter outputs shown.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 (panel A, Within one NVLink domain)
issue: Panel A's header time and the drawn topology encode different transfer models. Under TP=4 the KV is sharded four ways, so each GPU ships ~8.75 GB over its own 450 GB/s link and the transfer completes in ~0.02 s. The figure therefore simultaneously implies a per-GPU link and a whole-state-over-one-link time, and the reader cannot tell which model the 0.08 s belongs to.

figure: FIGURE 15.2(a) — Prefill work vs average prefix reuse (in-figure annotation)
issue: The figure's own parameters are undefined and insufficient to reproduce the curve. The annotation reads "f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%" but the caption never defines P or S, and the plotted curve is not f(r) — it is 100·[S + P·f(r)/f(1)], i.e. 60 + 80/(1+r). The normalization by f(1)=2.5 and the combination rule are both unstated, so a reader who tries to reproduce the curve from the annotation gets 5/(1+r) and cannot match the drawing. The reader also cannot tell why the curve floors at ~60 rather than 0 (the S=60% non-cacheable share of prefill), which is the single most decision-relevant feature of the curve.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 259: annotation "f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%". Caption describes only the axes and the meaning of "average prefix reuse"; it never mentions P, S, or f. Recomputation against the drawn curve: 100·[0.6 + 0.4·(5/(1+r))/(5/2)] = 60 + 80/(1+r) gives r=1→100, r=2→86.7, r=3→80, r=5→73.3, r=10→67.3, r=100→60.8, matching the drawn green curve (which flattens at ~60). The unnormalized f(r)=5/(1+r) would give 2.5 at r=1 and 0.05 at r=100, which does not match.
acceptance_test: Either (a) put the full formula in the figure annotation, e.g. "prefill work = S + P·f(r)/f(1); f(r)=5/(1+r), f(1)=2.5; P=40% cacheable, S=60% not cacheable", or (b) move the formula into the caption and define P and S there in words. Acceptance: a reader with only the figure and its caption can state what P and S mean, can reproduce the curve at r=1, 10 and 100, and can explain the ~60% floor.

issue: The x-axis mixes two rate bases without saying so. The caption states that the workload points are placed at "x = 10 rps average × duration," while the feasible-max boundary is "capacity 40 rps × 624,000 = 24.96M req/mo." The canonical point (6.24M) and the feasible max (24.96M) are therefore the SAME workload duration (624,000 s) at two different rates, not two volumes of the same workload. The axis label ("Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet") does not disclose this, so a reader can conclude that 24.96M req/mo is feasible for the canonical workload shape — which would require 2,496,000 active seconds, four times the 624,000 s window. The caption carries the correction; the figure does not.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 294: x-axis label "Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet". Caption assumptions: "x = 10 rps average × duration (for the workload points) ... feasible max = capacity 40 rps × 624,000 = 24.96M req/mo." Recomputation: 6,240,000 / 10 rps = 624,000 s (canonical duration); 24,960,000 / 10 rps = 2,496,000 s, which exceeds the 624,000 s active window by 4×.
acceptance_test: State the rate basis on the axis or in an in-figure note, e.g. "Requests/month (log) — workload points at 10 rps avg × duration; feasible max = 40 rps sustained × 624,000 s". Acceptance: the figure alone makes it impossible to read 24.96M as the same-workload volume that the canonical 6.24M point represents.

figure: FIGURE 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue: The BEFORE panel is annotated "O(L²) HBM traffic" while the AFTER panel carries no complexity label, which invites the false inference that FlashAttention is asymptotically cheaper in HBM traffic. It is not: with d fixed, naive attention is Θ(L²) HBM element-accesses and FlashAttention is Θ(L²d²/M) — the same order, with a constant-factor reduction set by on-chip SRAM capacity M. The caption's scope note ("the gain is fewer HBM round-trips, not a change to the attention mathematics") addresses the mathematics, not the asymptotics, so the misconception survives the caption. This is exactly the inference a reader is likely to carry into later capacity arithmetic.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 257: BEFORE annotation "O(L²) HBM traffic: L×L intermediate written + every query re-reads the KV rows"; AFTER annotation "KV reused per tile — no single global K/V pass; no L×L intermediate in HBM" with no complexity term. Caption: "the gain is fewer HBM round-trips, not a change to the attention mathematics (floating-point caveat ...)" — no statement about asymptotic order.
acceptance_test: Add an explicit complexity qualifier to the AFTER panel, e.g. "Θ(L²) HBM accesses with a constant-factor reduction set by on-chip capacity (d²/M)" (or an equivalent statement in the caption). Acceptance: the figure cannot be read as claiming an asymptotic reduction in HBM traffic, and the phrase "constant factor" or "d²/M" appears somewhere in the figure or its caption.

figure: FIGURE 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic (AFTER panel)
issue: The AFTER panel draws exactly two green arrows (one up, one down) between HBM and on-chip, labelled "few HBM round-trips." A reader can reasonably take two arrows as a fixed count of two HBM transfers, which is not what FlashAttention does: the number of HBM reads scales with the number of (query-block, KV-block) tile pairs. The caption's scope note explicitly disclaims this ("it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once globally across all query blocks"), but the figure itself carries no such qualifier — the qualifier lives only in prose, which is the wrong place for it given that the figure is the memorable artifact.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 257: AFTER panel shows one upward and one downward green arrow between the "on-chip" and "Q/K/V HBM" boxes, with the label "few HBM round-trips" to the left. Caption: "Scope of the 'read once' claim: the tile-level on-chip reuse is per-tile; it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once globally across all query blocks (the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile schedule, and SRAM size ...)."
acceptance_test: Qualify the arrow count in the figure itself — e.g. label the arrows "per tile" or add "arrows = per-tile transfers; count scales with # (Q-block, KV-block) tile pairs." Acceptance: the figure alone cannot be read as asserting a fixed number of HBM transfers.

figure: FIGURE 17.1 — Sizing a fleet by burst peak, headroom and failover (caption)
issue: The caption's sizing formula is not reproducible as printed: "the same formula gives N_min = ceil(ρ · 8.6) = 23 for the canonical pack, 22 with the reserve case (iii)". The figure's own basis (2.0 req/s per host) implies N_min = ceil(λ / (2.0 ρ)), which also does not produce 23 from 8.6. The reader is given a formula and a result that cannot both be true, and the figure's own capacity lines (2.0 / 6.0 / 8.0) do not bridge the gap.

figure: FIGURE 19.1 — The agent loop: a four-state machine
issue: The figure's legend states a different bounding mechanism from the caption's central claim. Caption: "Plan, Execute, Observe, Decide whose turn context budget, not the model's judgment, prevents an infinite loop." Figure legend: "resolved -> final answer; no resolution within the turn limit -> stopped", and the terminal edge is labelled "limit hit" with the box reading "limit / terminal". Nothing in the figure depicts a context or token budget; a reader who reads only the figure will conclude the loop is bounded by a turn counter, not by the context budget — the exact distinction the caption is making. The figure also omits the mechanism (context accumulation) that makes the budget bind.

Caption: "whose turn context budget, not the model's judgment, prevents an infinite loop. Assumption: an append-only context from the 9,200-token prompt at 2.62 MB/token KV (FP16)".
acceptance_test: The terminal edge is labelled with the budget (e.g. "context budget exhausted -> stopped") and the legend wording matches the caption's "turn context budget"; alternatively the caption is reworded to "turn limit". A reader can state from the figure alone which resource bounds the loop.

figure: FIGURE 19.2 — Agent turns: token and KV growth
issue: The figure note asserts a factor that the figure's own parameters do not produce: "tokens per submitted request grow 2.5x under no-prefix reuse (100-request ledger, Table 19-1)". From the figure's own stated inputs (9,200 input + 300 output + 800 + 65 per turn, 4 turns): with prefix reuse the request submits 9,200 + 300 + 4 x 865 = 12,960 tokens; without prefix reuse it submits the full context each turn, 10,365 + 11,230 + 12,095 + 12,960 = 46,650 tokens — a 3.6x ratio, not 2.5x. A benign reading exists (the 100-request ledger may use a different turn-count mix, which would change the ratio), but the note does not say so, so a reader who tries to reproduce 2.5x from the figure fails and cannot tell whether the figure or the ledger is wrong.
evidence: Rendered page 347 note: "tokens per submitted request grow 2.5x under no-prefix reuse (100-request ledger, Table 19-1)"; figure legend "initial context (I0)", "retrieved context (R)", "generated (Y=65)", "output (O=300)"; caption "(9,200 input + 300 output + 800 + 65 per turn)". Recomputation: 12,960 vs 46,650 -> 3.60x.
acceptance_test: The note states the turn-count mix behind the factor (e.g. "2.5x at the ledger's mean of X turns") and the factor is recomputed from that mix, or the factor is replaced by the figure-derivable 3.6x for the depicted 4-turn request. figure: Figure 22.1 (Attention vs. projection prefill FLOP crossover) — caption, first sentence
issue: The caption's takeaway concludes that at 128K the quadratic attention term 'is large but not yet dominant'. Under the figure's own full-square convention the quadratic term is already dominant at 128K (2.45x the linear term; 71% of total prefill FLOPs). Only under causal-triangle counting is it marginal (1.23x; 55%). The sentence chains both conventions into a single conclusion, so the reader is told the opposite of what the plotted crossover shows. This is the figure's headline takeaway and it is the claim most likely to be quoted downstream.
evidence: Recomputed from the figure's own formulas and the canonical geometry (N = 7e10 params, n_layers = 80, d = 8192): linear = 2NL = 2 x 7e10 x 131072 = 1.835e16 FLOP; quadratic (full-square) = 4 n_layers L^2 d = 4 x 80 x 8192 x 131072^2 = 4.504e16 FLOP -> quadratic/linear = 2.45, quadratic share of total = 71.0%. Causal-triangle: quadratic = 2.252e16 -> ratio 1.23, share 55.1%. The figure's own magenta annotation 'full-square quad overtakes ~53.4K' places the crossover at 53.4K < 128K, so the term must dominate at 128K under that convention. The parameter set is confirmed by reproducing the crossovers exactly: L = N/(2 n_layers d) = 7e10/(2 x 80 x 8192) = 53,405 tokens (full-square) and 106,810 tokens (causal-triangle), matching the printed ~53.4K and ~106.8K.
acceptance_test: Rewrite the takeaway to state the two conventions separately, e.g. 'at 128K the quadratic term is 2.5x the linear term under full-square counting (71% of prefill FLOPs) and 1.2x under causal-triangle counting (55%)'. Confirm the revised sentence is consistent with the ~53.4K / ~106.8K crossover annotations drawn in the plot, and that no other sentence in the chapter repeats the 'not yet dominant' claim.
